A novel approach has been devised for hadron decay analyses to generate probability distributions, leveraging artificial neural networks to enhance the accuracy of particle reconstruction. This method utilizes modern Monte Carlo simulations and employs a density estimation technique called adversarial neural density estimation. By training a neural network to mimic the shape of the probability distributions from simulated data, it was found that hadron decay decay spectra could be reconstructed with greater precision than current methods based on neural networks. Furthermore, this research demonstrated that density estimation represents a suitable application of adversarial neural networks for physics analyses and can be an efficient tool for exploring complex physical systems.

We have developed a novel radiative shock model that integrates both relativistic and non-relativistic afterglow phases into a single, unified framework. This model, based on ultra-relativistic and non-relativistic relativistic shock dynamics, accurately describes the post-short-duration-gravity-wave afterglow phenomena across all energy bands. Through numerical simulations, we have observed that the model effectively captures the transition phase, exhibiting universal scalar slopes of approximately 1.8 and 0.8 in the ultra-relativistic and non-relativistic regimes, respectively. We have further tested our model against multiple observed radiation patterns, including bright, short-duration radiation observed by the Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope and optical/near-infrared data from various telescopes. By simultaneously explaining both the early and late afterglow phases without requiring any free parameters, our model provides a comprehensive and self-consistent understanding of high-energy radiation produced by merging neutron star systems.

A bipartite graph can be visualized as having two distinct groups of connected nodes, represented by separate colors. Research indicates that splitting specific non-planar vertices can transform the graph into a planar format. To determine the minimum number of splits required, we need to identify the minimum number of non-planar vertices needed to make the graph planar. This study explores the scenario where the bipartite graph's planar representation includes overlapping edges and focuses on finding the smallest set of non-planar vertices needed to make the graph planar after splitting them. A key observation shows that this version can be used to solve the general problem, where the non-planar vertices are allowed to share edges with other non-planar vertices. A notable result reveals that if the bipartite graph contains no edges that cross each other, then the minimum number of non-planar vertices required to make it planar is equal to the number of its face boundaries. Additionally, an algorithm has been developed that can determine the required splits needed to make the graph planar within a cubic time complexity.

This paper explores the performance of a bipedal robot in a dynamic environment assisted by a sensor-enabled feedback control system. By entering into communication with its surroundings through a networking system, the robot receives real-time information about the objects near it and their effects on the feedback system. This enables the robot to adjust its behavior based on the effects of its actions on the environment. Through the application of the theory of external semiotics, we studied how the robot's performance improves due to closed-loop feedback during gait cycles. Additionally, we analyzed the robot's ability to adapt to its environment and other robots of the same kind through the exchange of signs. The results of these investigations will contribute to the development of efficient control systems and more adaptive robots.

We investigate the formal properties of an infinite field $F$ within the power series field $\kappa = F((t))$, specifically looking at $\kappa$ when it is endowed with a total residue map. This induces a valuation on $\kappa$, which in turn gives rise to a vector-like structure. We then examine the decision problem associated with this structure. If $F$ is finite, we find that this decision problem is r.e., whereas if $F$ is infinite, we discover that the problem becomes undecidable. Furthermore, we establish that this infinite problem does have a property called "recursively enumerable degree", which we believe could be more specifically characterized as "true $\Sigma_1^0$".

Exploiting hardware vulnerabilities to extract sensitive information from memory regions that have been evicted from the system's main memory, without direct access to these regions, presents significant technical challenges. To overcome these difficulties, researchers have developed techniques such as Flush+Reload attacks that leverage the caching mechanism to gain indirect insight into memory. However, the effectiveness of these attacks is limited by the need to acquire multiple system traces and the difficulty in determining when specific data was removed from memory. To address these challenges, a new approach has been developed that enhances the caching-based attack method by shortening the time required to pinpoint the memory removal event by up to 16 times and reducing the number of required system traces by up to 375 times. The improved technique, known as HyperDegrade, achieves these performance enhancements by introducing a novel caching state transition pattern that accelerates the removal detection event while increasing the difficulty of predicting when this event will occur. The effectiveness of HyperDegrade has been validated through real-world experiments and simulations, demonstrating its ability to efficiently extract sensitive information from memory without direct access, even in complex multi-core and cloud-based scenarios.

We introduce a new method to transform one type of knotted structure into another type, demonstrating how to convert a left-handed trefoil through a diagonal move, in a specific four-valved linked structure comprised of two trefoils and an figure-eight knotted component. This discovery provides the first known instance of a diagonal move being applied to a non-trivially linked trefoil and figure-eight knotted component, effectively linking it to the Grigahcine-O'Hayer linked structure that it mirrors.

For a specific family of knots known as hyperbolic knots, developing a method to calculate the volume can be achieved by combining two concepts: integrated simple closed surfaces and a particular type of cocycle. The goal of this study is to demonstrate that the Cayley graph's geometry derived from these combined elements is consistent with the definition of a ray in the solar system. As a result, this study provides an alternative approach to establishing that hyperbolic knots are non-trivial using combined integrated simple closed surfaces and cocycles. Furthermore, this approach can be used to create a new type of invariant for hyperbolic knots.

We introduce a new performance metric-specific optimization framework for tasks in a dynamic environment, where tasks have varying levels of difficulty and must be assigned to agents with distinct capabilities. We investigate two decision-making approaches for agent tasks: a naive strategy that prioritizes easy tasks and a optimal strategy that maximizes achievements based on task difficulty. We analyze these approaches in multiple scenarios with different task difficulty distributions. We also develop a computational agent model to test the effectiveness of our optimization framework through simulation.

This research undertakes a theoretical analysis of privacy vulnerabilities in vertical federated learning. We successfully implemented two privacy-breach attacks, one data-inference based attack and one machine-learning based attack, on top of two common vertical federated learning protocols. The results showed that privacy protection provided by vertical federated learning is insufficient and that sensitive information is readily accessible through certain data manipulations. To address this issue, we proposed an enhanced vertical federated learning framework, dubbed VFL-ENHANCED, which incorporates data encryption and utilizes encrypted neural networks, thereby significantly mitigating privacy breaches. We further probed the privacy-resilience of VFL-ENHANCED by launching the same attacks on this new protocol.

We introduce Pseudo-Random Fourier Features (PRFF), a newly developed method that builds upon the established Random Fourier Features (RFF) technique by leveraging similarities between data points to reduce the dimensionality of input spaces and facilitate efficient processing. Unlike RFF, PRFF creates a set of distinct, non-overlapping hyperballs centered on individual data points, with each ball corresponding to a unique set of Fourier weights. The proposed framework enhances RFF in various ways, enhancing both the reduced-dimension representation's accuracy and its efficiency. The PRFF approach exhibits improved performance, as demonstrated by our empirical evaluations, which include both a complex neural network and a linear neural network in multiple datasets, and matches the predictive power of the original input space while achieving substantial speedup and memory savings.

A key concept in the study of transformation groups acting on manifolds involves the Cartesian Decomposition (CC), a technique that enables the analysis of how a group's action affects a given space. The Diagonal Group (DG) is particularly significant because it represents a subset of regular group actions and is closely tied to CC. However, the original DG definition is only applicable to actions on product spaces, M X N, where both M and N share the same topological characteristics. The proposed research seeks to expand the DG framework to include actions on more complex spaces, like M X N X P X Q, where P and Q have distinct topological characteristics, thus providing a broader understanding of CC.

We establish an infinite family of compact conformally flat hypersurfaces in n-dimensional Euclidean space (n is 4 or higher) with specified positive scalar curvature and specific dimensional parameters. These surfaces fill a wide range of dimensions, including all even numbers greater than 4, and their surface area can be minimized under certain constraints. Additionally, we demonstrate that these optimal surfaces have a specific constant mean curvature and are chemically stable. Furthermore, we prove that they have a specific integral geometry property and that their surface area dimension follows a specific power law in relation to a scaling factor.

A new strategy is proposed to address the challenge of power transfer and data transmission in wireless networks, involving time-divided and power-splitting techniques. The technique, which allows a single RF path for simultaneous data transmission and energy harvesting, has been the subject of recent research. However, the issue of antenna switching was not effectively addressed in these studies, despite its potential benefits. The research presented here develops an optimization problem to maximize energy efficiency in a single-carrier wireless network using the generalized antenna-switching technique. The findings of the research, conducted in an OFDM context with multiple carriers, show that the same solution can be applied to an increased number of carriers. Moreover, the results demonstrate that the proposed technique leads to a significant increase in energy efficiency. The proposed model is also shown to be compatible with other optimization problems.

We investigated the spread of damage through a percolating network that breaks apart into distinct clusters when a random connection is removed. Our study focused on the impact of removing a single node that leads to the collapse of multiple clusters. We found that the size of this network failure can be significantly reduced by removing a random node before the network's initial state is established. Our primary research explored how the size of network failures changes when a single node is removed repeatedly. Our results showed that the distribution of failure sizes follows a power law, but only over a limited range, before entering an exponential phase. This phenomenon can be observed in both square and triangular lattice networks. In contrast, networks with node removals based on random variables or according to a specific distance rule exhibit exponential distributions of failure sizes. We also discovered that the size of failures does not significantly change when the network is large, but it can be influenced by the bond-percolation threshold. In networks with multiple components, the size of failures is directly related to the component sizes. Our research found that the distribution of failure sizes can be influenced by the network's initial state, but only over a narrow range.

We've developed a novel gravitational wave detector concept called the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer, which significantly boosts sensitivity by combining a rotating interferometer with a non-fixed end mirror. This design surpasses the performance of a standard Michelson interferometer with the same optical components, offering improved sensitivity of about a factor of 1.16 times, specifically in the low-frequency regime. Additionally, this design provides enhanced sensitivity in the high-frequency regime, with an estimated improvement of 5 dB compared to the standard Michelson design. These findings have been verified numerically and validated through practical testing using our laboratory-scale sloshing-Sagnac interferometer.

This study proposes a new random access (RA) protocol called NOVR-XL for XL-MIMO systems. XL-MIMO systems involve multiple antennas at both the base station and mobile devices, leading to a significant increase in random access traffic. To address this challenge, we designed NOVR-XL to minimize the number of RA transmissions while considering antenna weighting factors. By doing so, NOVR-XL achieves a 37.5% reduction in RA transmissions and a 25% increase in throughput compared to the existing NOVR protocol.

A protoplanetary disk's inner region remains uninhabited by planets due in part to a lack of suitable grain growth sites. If substructures in protoplanetary disks can trap particles, facilitating their growth, then perhaps the newly formed grains could aggregate into larger particles, ultimately becoming planetesimals that could create the cores for planets. To explore this idea, we examine the millimeter interstellar medium substructures adjacent to the Taurus Star Formation Region using a combined analysis of continuum and CO data. A total of 119 ridges were identified within the region, with at least 50 of these ridges displaying density increases of over 50 standard deviations above their surrounding environment when mapped at 1.3 arcsecond resolutions. If even a fraction of these substructures can influence planet formation, then it's likely that most formed planets would exhibit unusual, aligned orbits. To observe this phenomenon, we conducted an aligned orbit search among 459 known gas-rich planet candidates within the Taurus Star Formation Region and surrounding areas. As expected, we discovered that planets with aligned orbits are rare, with aligned orbital alignments occurring in less than 3.5% of candidate planets. Notably, one significant alignment was found within the Taurus Star Formation Region with a reported orbital alignment of 7.5 degrees and a orbital period of approximately 20 days with its host star being a 0.46 solar masses star.

Recently, a new energy density functional known as BigApple has been created for use in nuclear many-body problems. Originating from a modified Gogny-Hartree-Fock approach with a unique set of forces, BigApple serves as a straightforward and effective interaction for the collective degree of freedom. To further utilize its capabilities, BigApple has been applied within the Landau liquid theory to its maximal extent by calculating nuclear matter properties at various finite temperature levels. The resulting global properties, including the incompressibility, symmetry energy, and equation of state, are in excellent agreement with established experimental values and empirical formulas. The underlying microscopic information from the BigApple functional at the level of individual nucleons has been examined through a nuclear matter density distribution analysis. The obtained results can be utilized as a reference for finite temperature finite range interactions and will contribute to advancing our understanding of nuclear matter and its finite size counterparts.

Our investigation focuses on frequency-robust Molmer-Sorensen gates, analyzing their performance under realistic conditions and comparing different designs to facilitate accumulation of entanglement within ion chains. Due to inevitable fluctuations in motivation amplitude, duration, and shape, we consider robust implementations of these gates, emphasizing their potential for sustained, complex quantum dynamics. Our study, conducted via numerical simulations of actual quantum trajectories, reveals that well-designed robust Molmer-Sorensen gates can induce extensive and localized entanglement in middle-length chains of ions, paving the way for utilization in quantum simulations of intricate chemical reactions and molecular resonance phenomena.

A recently discovered material, GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$, is highly fascinating due to its unprecedented combination of properties, including a rare Dirac cone structure and strong electron-phonon coupling. Theoretical analysis indicates that this material also exhibits positive compressibility, a feature that contradicts conventional wisdom about the interplay between electron-phonon coupling and compressibility. Theoretical simulations predict that this material may display an unusual metal-to-insulator phase transition at finite temperature, a phenomenon driven by its unique band structure. This discovery opens the door to investigating many-body physics and the nature of the phase transition in this novel material.

The search for heavy neutral leptons is a well-established and versatile area of investigation that can be explored through various experiments beyond the current particle physics facilities. In this study, we examine potential discoveries or more precise limits for heavy neutral leptons with masses ranging from a few hundred MeV to 1 TeV in the neutrino sector, and from a few hundred MeV to 50 TeV in the charged lepton sector. We evaluated the optimal sensitivities for heavy neutral leptons through the analysis of various processes in high-energy colliders and other experiments, taking into consideration factors like existing limitations, potential breakthroughs, and the effectiveness of different production processes. We also outline strategies for enhancing the effectiveness of certain experiments and identify areas where future research or more detailed studies are necessary.

This paper introduces a new hybrid language model called Semi-Supervised Expanded Encoder, which builds on the success of prior approaches that combine basic n-gram models with advanced neural language models. By leveraging the strengths of both models, our hybrid approach achieves significant improvements in language tasks like machine translation and summarization, as seen in our experiment results. Specifically, when applied to the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, our model delivers a notable 1.1% boost in translation accuracy compared to the original baseline, surpassing the performance of lattice-based training, which requires vast amounts of prior data. Additionally, our hybrid model demonstrates enhanced performance in abstractive news summarization, exceeding the results achieved with standard neural model benchmarks by 3.6% in ROUGE-1 score and 5.6% in ROUGE-2 score when using the DUC 2004 dataset.

Reconstructing a three-dimensional face begins with estimating both face-dependent and independent components. However, current methods primarily concentrate on separating these components from a single input image, neglecting the significant information present in images of the subject's face from different viewpoints. In this research, we introduce the Self-aligned Dual face Regression Network (SADRNet), a unique framework specifically designed to accommodate multiple view-dependent face images. These images, despite being from various poses, share a common origin, allowing for the separation of pose-independent factors and the estimation of pose-dependent factors for each view. This is achieved through a proposed dual regression mechanism where each view is treated as an independent regression problem, and the network is trained to forecast both components across different poses by maximizing cross-view consistency. The primary component is then re-rendered using a proposed facial alignment technique that aligns the rendered faces without the need for manual alignment, enabling the network to focus solely on intrinsic geometric features. This is, in turn, used to adapt the network to novel, unseen poses. This novel approach enables the generation of three-dimensional faces from limited pose-dependent and pose-independent factors, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods in reconstruction accuracy according to our experiments.

Researchers examined the scalar power spectrum and its impact on the Bardeen potential's behavior, specifically focusing on situations where a significant portion of the Bardeen potential takes on very negative values. To achieve this analysis, they employed a Gaussian perturbation as a initial condition for the Bardeen potential. By carrying out numerical power spectrum calculations, it was discovered that a sharp, positive slope in the Bardeen potential's power spectrum spectrum occurs when a negative value of the potential is generated with a magnitude greater than 5, with this feature becoming sharper as the standard deviation of the perturbation decreases. A related, simpler model involving a linear potential also showed similar results.

Researchers examined the distribution of the number of deepest nodes in standard ordered trees and found it increases with the size of the tree, with an estimated rate of $1.98967$, when the tree size is very large. This rate was determined by analyzing the expected value of the number of deepest nodes under the uniform distribution on standard ordered trees. As a point of comparison, the same analysis for marked ordered trees yielded an estimated rate of $2.00054$. These findings are significant because the number of deepest nodes in standard ordered trees can be viewed as a non-homogeneous Markov chain, with a stationary distribution that correlates with the uniform distribution. This connection was utilized to determine the rate at which the height of a random standard ordered tree grows, which was previously an unknown value.

Accuracy of optical character recognition (OCR) is not exceptionally high in manual vote tabulation, leading to the potential need for human-corrected character recognition output being further processed to ensure voting data accuracy. To enhance this process, this research proposes a spell-checking-based post-OCR correction method. Utilizing standard spell-checking techniques, the algorithm compares the recognized characters against a dictionary of valid entry options and selects the most suitable match. To accommodate variations in voting data entry, the algorithm was designed to utilize an "ignore" option for words not found in the dictionary, effectively mimicking the freedom of post-OCR correction by human operators. Evaluating the proposed spell-checking-based post-OCR correction algorithm on real-world voting data, the results showed a significant improvement in accuracy, with an overall char-level accuracy increasing from 85.4% without correction to 97.2% with the proposed method.

Linear models that operate beyond their parameterized dimensions can provide highly effective solutions for categorizing vast amounts of data. Nonetheless, training such models presents a challenge, as their optimization issue involves a linear task with countless variables that change over time and must be resolved within a finite duration. To tackle this issue, researchers have developed an optimization approach that employs continuous time grids to train the model. This method has been proven to yield highly desirable theoretical properties, as it guarantees that the model's error rate decreases at a logarithmic rate in proportion to the number of time points used. To expand on this research, an alternative algorithm has been discovered that is capable of producing similar results by leveraging a more efficient time division structure.

As distribution grid management policies become more nuanced in low-carbon energy systems, the risk-averse nature of storage resources has the potential to significantly impact their participation in the market. This study develops a stochastic dual long-term framework that incorporates risk-averse storage operators into their decision-making process. By examining the inherent risk preferences of storage resources within this framework, our results reveal that risk-averse storage operators tend to prioritize shorter-term risks over longer-term ones. Furthermore, our findings suggest that such risk-averse behavior could either mitigate or contribute to voltage risks and renewable energy curtailment, depending on specific grid conditions. Our research also provides a risk-adjusted storage efficiency metric that can be utilized by grid managers in informing management policies and managing voltage risks and renewable energy curtailment in low-carbon energy systems.

Using a reduced gravity, global, and simple atmospheric model, we studied an Earth-like atmosphere with a substantial hydrogen wind and a polar ice cap. The model revealed recurring mid-latitude storm patterns and a stable circulation around the polar region, mirroring observations on Mars. The similar circulation patterns on Mars and in our model suggest that the atmospheric conditions that generated baroclinic storms on Mars are plausible in an Earth-like atmosphere of the past. The model also demonstrated how the precipitation patterns and polar atmospheric circulation could have evolved over time, ultimately leading to ice cap loss and surface liquid water. The model's results agree with previous studies conducted using more complex atmospheric models but were easier to understand and visualize in our reduced gravity model.

Traditional active learning algorithms often employ nearest neighbors as query candidates, selecting those with the most uncertain classifications for further inspection. Despite its simplicity, this approach has been effective in various active learning settings, yet our research reveals that it struggles with larger, more complex image datasets, such as ImageNet. In contrast, the best results are achieved when the most distinguishing features from a dataset are identified and used to determine which samples require verification. However, this more adaptive strategy is more computationally intensive. Repeating our experiments on previous large-scale image datasets, we found that the current ResNet model falls short in accurately predicting the active learning strategy most effective for these datasets. Consequently, our research will be focused on improving the model's performance through the implementation of various data augmentation techniques during training.

Researchers utilize classical electrodynamics to explain how the position and sensitivity of donor atoms in silicon can be adjusted to enhance two-qubit logic operations involving phosphorus dopants. By analyzing various gate configurations, they found that modifying the electrical connection between qubits through a nearby donor atom can significantly improve coherence time, reduce calibration needs, and enhance two-qubit logic performance. Specifically, they showed that increasing the distance between the two-qubit system and a nearby donor atom can significantly decrease the amplitude of unwanted two-qubit interactions, thus improving the reliability of two-qubit logic operations involving these systems.

Researchers from the University of Geneva and the University of Neuchâtel have observed unusual resistance fluctuations in silicon macroscopic samples under a strong magnetic field. Unlike previous observations in Germanium samples, the resistance oscillations occurred immediately after the Landau level at the zero energy point, which is typically inaccessible due to scattering events lifting the degeneracy in quantum wells. The findings are explained by a scattering theory that takes into account the spatial distribution of electrons in the conduction band along with the spin and orbital components, which were previously overlooked. By applying a novel analysis developed by Dr. G. A. Bastard, the researchers were able to extract precise scattering durations and lifetimes from the resistance fluctuations. The discovered values agree with experimental data on the electric mobility and provide new insights into the behavior of free electrons in a strong magnetic field along a silicon quantum well.

A proposed algorithm is introduced to address power allocation and scheduling in dynamic Time Division Duplex (TDD) systems by utilizing sample average approximation and multi-armed bandit feedback effectively. The solution utilizes an $\epsilon$-greedy strategy in combination with power level rounding to facilitate efficient data collection and accurate estimation of optimal solutions. The resulting algorithm achieves optimal throughput performance and reduced computation costs. The efficacy of the proposed solution is demonstrated through simulations in various scenarios.

In this study, we test the proposed Hamiltonian Neural Network against an
established baseline, specifically an LSTM-based meta-learner, in the context of
two well-known tasks: the MNIST dataset for physics inference and the CMU face
dataset for physics-based animation. According to the results obtained through the
Testing Trajectory Generator module, HNN outperforms the baseline in both cases.
Moreover, we observe that HNN is capable of accurately identifying the correct
model parameters even when given rise to by flawed or incomplete initial state
inputs. Additionally, the introduced Hamiltonian Neural Network demonstrates the
potential to achieve comparable accuracy when compared to a meta-learning based
approach in a scenario involving the MNIST dataset for physics inference, while
it achieves significant improvements over the baseline in a scenario involving the
CMU face dataset for physics-based animation.

In a collaborative setting, multiple agents can work together to achieve a common goal by exchanging information and machine learning models. This study explores a new approach to cooperative learning, termed chain cooperative learning, where multiple agents take turns sharing their models with each other. The key aspects of this approach are as follows: cooperative learning occurs in a linear sequence where agents share their current model with the next agent in the chain; the recipient agent updates its model based on the received model and sends the updated model to the previous agent in the chain; this process is repeated until the initial agent receives the shared model back and updates it with the help of the other agents. The proposed chain cooperative learning model can be adapted to different scenarios, such as multiple agents cooperating with each other, an agent cooperating with multiple instances of itself, and an agent cooperating with different instances of itself with changing parameters. Moreover, this model can facilitate secure learning where the sharing of models is done securely among agents. This study also provides theoretical proof that chain cooperative learning can enhance the accuracy of machine learning models and boost the trust score when compared to individual learning. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through practical examples, showing that chain cooperative learning can lead to significant improvements in model accuracy and trust score when compared to the conventional machine learning approach.

A recently introduced polynomial invariant from the $J_n$ family, specifically $J_n^T$, does not provide distinct invariants for distinct links when the number of crossings exceeds 11. Our research extends this lack of distinction to 16 crossings or more.

The efficacy of data augmentation methods in enhancing the performance of deep learning models on certain NLP tasks has been consistently demonstrated. While initially used primarily to enlarge training datasets, data augmentation techniques have now been employed with significant success in various tasks beyond sentence-level manipulation. This paper delves into an in-depth exploration of the applications of data augmentation in modeling word meanings and phrases, as well as the potential challenges and areas of future research as data augmentation continues to evolve. We examine multiple approaches to data augmentation, including sentence-level manipulation, character-level innovation, multi-task learning, autoencoder-inspired methods, and advances in LMT, all while providing concrete empirical evidence to support our claims. We also present possible future research directions, including the incorporation of semantic aspects, the utilization of external resources, and the exploration of alternative architectures. This comprehensive survey is set to contribute significantly to the ongoing discussion on effective data augmentation techniques in NLP.

The complex Gamma function's representation through the Hankel path connects the upper and lower halves of the complex plane. This path starts in the upper half-plane, curves around the left in a circle, continues into the lower half-plane, curves around the right in a circle, and returns to the upper half-plane. We have discovered that this path can be replaced with a straight line connecting points in the upper and lower half-planes without affecting the outcome. This discovery enables the derivation of an infinite product representation for the Gamma function along the Hankel path, which can be useful in analyzing the function's properties, especially in relation to the Riemann hypothesis and the distribution of prime numbers.

An analysis of top quark production in proton collisions is performed using data from the STAR experiment from energies of 200 GeV to 8.16 TeV, covering cross section ranges of 1.2 pb to 88 pb. The measured values are compared to theoretical predictions from various methods of quantum chromodynamics, demonstrating alignment with theoretical estimates across all energy levels. Specifically, cross section measurements at lower energies (below 1 TeV) align with predictions from fixed-order calculations, while higher energy energies are better explained by merged calculations that account for particle collisions.

Our proposed method addresses several issues arising from the limited availability of database information, including incomplete, outdated, and missing data. To tackle this challenge, we develop a unique approach that combines the benefits of descriptive and procedural knowledge to enhance application functionality. By integrating descriptive and procedural knowledge, our system achieves superior results in the absence of complete database information. In such cases, our framework relies on procedural knowledge to provide meaningful responses and accurate instructions for resolving inconsistencies and gaps in the database. Furthermore, we demonstrate how our proposed technique precludes the necessity for specialized handling of null values and how it facilitates seamless integration with existing applications. In addition, we present specific implementation details of our proposed method, including how it handles join operations and handles scenarios with missing join information.

Machine learning models that effectively handle complex relationships between input data often employ graph-based representations to capture these relationships. However, incorporating differential privacy into such models reveals a significant challenge in calculating privacy breaches due to the interconnected nature of the data points, which makes previous analytical approaches unsuitable. In our analysis, we first illustrate how to calculate privacy breaches correctly in a variety of interconnected scenarios, including connected components, graph interconnectedness, and interconnected scenarios with multiple datasets. We then derive an optimized approach for private learning on graph-structured data, incorporating a novel measure of interconnectedness that significantly reduces privacy breaches while complying with standard constraints. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by incorporating the measure of interconnectedness into popular private learning algorithms. Our results show that this approach yields significantly lower privacy breaches, which can also be measured as an increase in model accuracy.

The Euclid mission's extensive astronomical and cosmological research portfolio will greatly benefit from its comprehensive sky surveys. At its core, Euclid will conduct two regular, wide-field observations: one in the visible light spectrum with a 0.86 degrees field of view and another in the near-infrared spectrum with a 10 degrees field of view. Combining these observations will result in high-resolution images of an approximately 15,000 square degree field, allowing for in-depth studies in various areas, including the structure and evolution of the local group of galaxies, galaxy evolution and formation, and cosmological and dark energy research. Furthermore, Euclid's sensitive near-infrared observations will lead to discoveries in areas previously inaccessible, paving the way for significant breakthroughs in the field.

Quantum hydrodynamics is employed to simulate non-equilibrium quantum corrections in positron-electron plasma.  A linearized stochastic hydrodynamic model significantly outperforms existing methods for both lattice-based and traditional simulations in reducing quantum fluctuations' non-equilibrium effects.  In order to enhance the model's efficiency, adjustments are made to the stochastic time-stepping method, resulting in a linearized model that minimizes the impact of non-equilibrium quantum corrections while maintaining accurate equilibrium quantum corrections.  The optimized model is subsequently applied to evaluate quantum corrections within an intense electron pulse, as well as in thin, warm plasma layers undergoing breakdown, and the results are compared to alternative approaches and experimental data with satisfactory agreement.

We investigate the probabilistic properties of a renewal process whose jump lengths have independent and identically distributed distributions, with variable exponents characterizing the tail behavior. Specifically, we analyze the distant aspects of the process and its associated letter sequence, which is generated by mapping each renewal time to a random letter based on the time elapsed since the last jump occurred. This leads to a quenching limit for the letter sequence's distribution, which is equivalent to a random walk with independent and identically distributed step distributions with varying tail exponents. By examining the distant aspects of this walk, we establish both a quenched and an unbiased large deviation principle for the letter sequence's distribution. Furthermore, we outline the distinct phases of the quenching limit, which are influenced by the tail exponents of the original distributions and include the subexponential, light-tailed, and superexponential phases.

If a map f: S to M is relatively 1-homotopic between manifolds M and S of certain dimensions, we can find a 1-dimensional chain of maps from S to M that are all homotopic to f. This concept is significant because it enables us to use it as a key component in a proof about the existence of a specific type of map. Building on the earlier work by the second-listed author, where it was proved that there are no relatively 1-homotopic maps from the sphere SN to the manifold M if the manifold M has a specific property and N is greater than 3, we can now extend this finding to include the case N = 3. In this case, we also establish that the second homotopy group of M is trivial. As a result, we can demonstrate that any relatively 1-homotopic map from SN to M is actually homotopic to a map that we can define as r ∘ f, where r: SN to SN is a specific reflection map. This allows us to prove that there are no relatively 1-homotopic maps from S^3 to the Gr(2,4)-manifold M_2 four.

Recent studies on 64Ni utilizing the RIBF-RIA and the DRC+ reaction code investigated energetic excitations within this stable-nucleus nucleus. By examining two-proton removal reactions, researchers were able to extract excitational levels and study how they evolve in relation to the N=40 neutron subshell gap and the monopole interaction. Initial research on 64Ni focused primarily on bound states; however, excitational levels above the neutron subshell gap were not well understood. To address this knowledge gap, the RIBF-RIA utilized a 84Kr beam to collide with 28Si targets, producing 64Ni nuclei that were then studied through two-proton removal reactions. By analyzing these reactions, scientists were able to determine probable two-proton configurations, study the movement of protons and neutrons relative to each other, and explore energetic excitational levels above the neutron subshell gap. Equilibrium and non-equilibrium excitational levels were examined and compared to theoretical predictions from the DRC+ reaction code and the GCM-BkB theoretical model.

J-K-fold cross-validation is an emerging technique that involves dividing a dataset into K subgroups and then performing J-fold validation within each subgroup. This method provides more stable performance estimates than standard K-fold cross-validation due to its reduced reliance on random sampling. However, the benefits of J-K-fold cross-validation come with a higher computational cost resulting from the need for repeated random sampling within each subgroup. This study investigates the relationship between the number of subgroups (K) and the number of folds (J) for optimal performance, as previous research has not explored this thoroughly. Experimental results indicate that both larger K and J values lead to more stable performance estimates, although the optimal combination varies depending on the specific problem. Interestingly, this study also discovered instances where J-K-fold cross-validation yields poorer performance compared to standard K-fold cross-validation. Consequently, researchers and practitioners are advised to approach J-K-fold cross-validation with caution and carefully consider its benefits and drawbacks.

Recently introduced Teacher-Student architectures provide our understanding of how a lightweight student network can excel compared to a sophisticated teacher network. Nonetheless, multiple possible implementations exist and aren't mutually exclusive, necessitating a comprehensive exploration to identify the most effective approaches. In this paper, we investigate various implementations of Teacher-Student architectures, including both non-equivalent and equivalent training methods for students and teachers, and thoroughly examine their performance in multiple dataset scenarios. Furthermore, we leverage knowledge distillation modules as part of our evaluation, presenting three novel combinations and assessing their performance in both non-equivalent and equivalent settings. Our results demonstrate that only a handful of methods achieve performance comparable to the original network, and suggest areas for potential improvement in widely adopted baselines. This work is accompanied by the release of our DSSD code hub, offering convenient access to our lightweight network implementations.

By integrating various inference and optimization techniques into a unified framework known as Bucket Elimination, researchers have provided a significant improvement in efficiency for certain graphical models. Originally conceived as a sophisticated elimination algorithm, Bucket Elimination was discovered to be equivalent to other established methods, including Survey Propagation and Recursive Convolutional Codes. Additionally, the Bucket Elimination framework facilitates innovative optimizations, as demonstrated in a specific scenario where it was used to enhance Word Sense Disambiguation using a multilayered cognitive architecture.

At high intensities, strong absorption of light results in a shift in frequency due to the emitted photon's momentum, causing a distinctive lineshape when a single absorption process is considered. However, when multiple absorption processes occur simultaneously, the interaction becomes more complex and the resulting spectrum cannot be reduced to a simple shift in frequency. Using a classical electromagnetic model, researchers have observed the formation of sidebands in a two-photon absorption lineshape, despite being narrowly focused on a specific scenario. In contrast, our analysis of a more comprehensive two-level, one-photon absorption scenario reveals that the frequency shift is negligible, causing sideband suppression and a transformation of the lineshape to a double peak. In addition to the permanent frequency shift induced by the absorbed/emitted photon's momentum, a temporary and reversible frequency shift also occurs as a result of the absorber's initial/state change, which can be thought of as a light- matter entanglement phenomenon, and has never been previously reported.

Recent advances in simulating granular materials using discrete element methods have enabled the study of jamming phenomena across various dimensions. By applying these methods to investigate three-dimensional jamming under the influence of friction, researchers found that the universal characteristics of frictionless isotropic jamming are preserved while introducing Coulomb friction leads to a distinct phase of shear jamming. The results of this study, obtained through extensive numerical simulations, reveal the existence of two independent exponents characterizing frictional shear jamming. Notably, the specific values of these exponents differ significantly from those observed in the absence of friction, thereby demonstrating the distinct nature of shear jamming. The occurrence of shear jamming was previously inferred through the non-monotonic behavior of the shear modulus with respect to temperature, and further analysis has shed light on the underlying mechanisms driving this phenomenon. Ultimately, the findings of this research are seen as crucial steps towards better understanding the complex behavior of granular materials and other jammed materials that exhibit non-linear responses to stress.

We develop the centralizer $Z(n)^{(2)}$ within the Lie algebra of the superloop gl(1|1) and comprehensively characterize its components. Subsequently, we demonstrate how to apply the Hilbert-Poincaré method to the adjacency algebra of the double loop braid group D(B(2)). Moreover, we examine the characteristics of the centralizer $Z(n)^{(2)}$ through a detailed analysis of its Hilbert-Poincaré series. This investigation yields a comprehensive set of equations to determine the series of $Z(n)^{(2)}$, followed by a constructive approach to obtaining the dimension of the centralizer's irreducible components. Ultimately, these components' series are expressed in a simplified form, facilitating an in-depth examination of the assembly's composition.

Public sector professionals heavily rely on Google's search engine for
information, but they must also consider the potential for algorithmic
disparities in Web search results, including biases affecting similar queries
with different meanings. This article explores the implications of such
disparities for decision-making in the public sector and highlights the need
for a more critical approach to using Web search results in official contexts.

We propose a TeV-scale muon collider with energies ranging from a few TeV to 14 TeV and outline two possible design scenarios with beam powers of 1 E/A or 4 E/A, where E represents the energy and A is a measure of the luminosity. We examine various particle production processes, including Standard Model (SM) reactions, beyond SM phenomena, and dark matter production, in both design scenarios using the Delphini code. Our study demonstrates that a muon collider can accommodate multiple research objectives simultaneously. In the high-energy regime, it can efficiently probe contact interactions and produce massive vectors, such as gluons and leptons. At lower energies, it can also investigate composite Higgs scenarios, leptoquarks, and dark matter theories. We have not explored certain areas, such as little Higgs models and extra gauge bosons, which may also be accessible with this collider concept.

A novel sampling technique known as rCASPR sampling has been developed for improving image reconstruction in MRI, particularly for fast and accurate T2 relaxation time mapping. rCASPR intentionally broadens the point-spread function of the sampling pattern by increasing interpolation requirements, however, this increase is demonstrated to occur locally, allowing for sparse, randomly distributed sampling without significant losses in image contrast when using SPIP reconstruction. A proposed model was validated through simulation data and shown to accurately match the expected point-spread function of rCASPR, even outperforming traditional linear sampling in this regard. Additionally, the benefits of rCASPR were successfully translated to real-world applications through the conduct of T2 relaxation time mapping scans on human subjects utilizing ultra-fast, free-breathing acquisition protocols with both rCASPR-SPIP and traditional linear sampling-SPIP methods. The resulting T2 relaxation time maps demonstrated a clear improvement in quality with the rCASPR sampling method.

We introduce an exact algorithm designed to address the paired-permutation test issue formulated by Bergsma and Hung (2010), which significantly outperforms the Monte Carlo approximation described in Qiu et al. (2019) in terms of efficiency. We also provide a theoretical proof establishing the optimal time complexity of this exact algorithm. We then demonstrate the superior performance of this exact algorithm through comparative experiments conducted using real-world data sets.

Recently introduced legislation in the US seeks to promote fair competition in shipping industries previously controlled by cartels. This study evaluates the effects of the Shipping Act of 1916, specifically section 6(f), which prohibited shipping companies from entering into certain agreements that could limit competition. To analyze the outcomes of this section, we used a stochastic game model to investigate how changes in freight rates and shipping quantities result from different shipping company strategies. Our findings show that companies would ideally collaborate to achieve higher profits, but this cooperation is challenging due to trust issues and potential betrayals. In fact, our research discovered that shipping companies prioritized short-term gains over longer-term relationships. Following the enforcement of section 6(f), we found that it led to increased freight rates and shipping quantities immediately. However, as companies became more risk-averse, freight rates eventually decreased while shipping quantities increased in the long term. Notably, our research revealed that section 6(f) led to lower freight rates and higher shipping quantities in the long run. Consequently, we believe that fair competition policies are more effective in shipping industries than fair sharing of profits.

We introduce a new class of topological spaces called "loom spaces" that possess a specific structural property. These spaces share triangulations characterized by local structures akin to lemniscates, providing a fundamental understanding of their topological nature. This discovery leads to the categorization of loom spaces within the broader context of locally convex spaces. Furthermore, we identify relationships between loom spaces and other recognized topological spaces, including dendritic spaces and locally polyhedral spaces. These connections reveal that spaces belonging to the loom category also belong to these other categories, however the converse is not necessarily true.

The continuous flow of publicly available data necessitates the development of methods to quickly process high volumes of information. Technical indicators and historical stock prices are widely accessible stocks' past data, influencing their future behavior. This paper employs a convolutional neural network to analyze various technical indicators and historical price patterns, accurately predicting stock price movements in the Singapore stock market. Experimental results show that, compared to traditional regression methods, this convolutional neural network delivers superior performance, indicating that CNN effectively captures nonlinear relationships in stock price data.

We have created a new Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) to describe the double Higgs boson production and decay processes. Using the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) as a basis, we identified the most significant coefficients influencing these processes and mapped their relationships. Subsequently, we re-expressed the HEFT in a form that parallels the SMEFT, thereby linking the effective operators in both frameworks. This connection enables us to compare the LHC constraints on the HEFT and SMEFT, finding that the latter imposes more stringent requirements on certain coefficients, specifically those related to the dimension-five operator involving the Higgs doublet fields. Nevertheless, the SMEFT constraints are generally less stringent than the HEFT for the dimension-six operators related to gauge sectors and the effective operator involving a lepton and a Higgs field. We have also explored the mass invariants available in single Higgs production within the HEFT and SMEFT, establishing that the SMEFT offers a more comprehensive analysis, with the HEFT constrained by specific threshold corrections that the SMEFT cannot detect. Ultimately, we propose that the SMEFT should be utilized as the primary effective theory for Higgs physics at the LHC, given its more comprehensive dimension-five operator analysis and equivalent dimension-six operator constraints.

We've developed a novel approach to achieving an analytical expansion in general relativity by introducing the 'pre-non-relativistic' parametrization, which allows for the inclusion of relativistic effects in gravitational phenomena. This method overcomes the limitations of other approximation techniques and provides a clear framework for incorporating higher-order relativistic corrections. By utilizing the 'pre-non-relativistic' parametrization, we've successfully applied the multiple-scale method to create a perturbative expansion for a static, point-like, self-gravitating system in the presence of an external, weak, background field. This expansion can be extended to higher orders and we've identified the criteria for its validity. Additionally, we've derived the corresponding relativistic corrections to Newton's law and identified the factors that limit the effectiveness of the approximation. This research paves the way for further exploration into the application of this 'pre-non-relativistic' parametrization in more complex scenarios.

We investigated the drag experienced by a cylindrical intruder moving through granular beds at various speeds and depths, using both high-speed cameras and force sensors. The results show that the drag experienced by the intruder depends on its speed, size, and the properties of the surrounding grains, but not on its depth. The drag measurements vary significantly from those predicted by established models, which overestimate the effect of speed and bed depth. The actual drag experienced by the intruder can be explained by a simplified model that takes into account the formation of a granular flow layer above it, but only at high speeds. At low speeds, the flow behaves differently, resulting in much lower drag.

Our study examined the connection between triangular flow, or "triangle flow," and elliptic flow within mid-speed proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. We compared the speed dependencies of triangle and elliptic flows from identified particles, such as pions, kaons, and protons. We found that triangle flow exhibits a similar transverse momentum dependence as elliptic flow, specifically displaying a comparable mass number that is roughly half as large. This discovery could be explained by similar flow generation mechanisms or by distinct mechanisms that also result in similar speed ratios. Furthermore, triangle and elliptic flows demonstrated a nearly identical transverse momentum range, indicating that triangle flow does not experience a reduction typically seen in elliptic flow. This research also enabled us to revisit previous studies on mass number and transverse momentum dependencies of triangle flow.

An examination of rare $B$ meson decay phenomena, particularly sensitive to new physics, is summarized with an emphasis on $B^0_s \to \mu^+ \mu^-$ and $B^0 \to \mu^+ \mu^-$ decays. We interconnect experimental findings from various collaborations, citing key results, along with theoretical understanding from various approaches, including Light Cone Sum Rules, Form Factor extraction via Davydov methods, and Quark Level calculations. We also discuss potential future discoveries and precision requirements at future facilities, such as the LHCb Upgrade and the Super T2KK experiment.

We introduce a novel iteration method called FGMRES-D, which is a modification of the standard finite-element generalized minimal residual iteration preconditioned by a direct method. The proposed approach enhances the standard FGMRES iteration by employing an approximate Jacobian matrix in the process. The impact of this approximation on the iteration process is then analyzed. Additionally, the proposed method is compared to the standard FGMRES iteration in terms of computational efficiency. The results of these comparisons are presented in the form of numerical experiments conducted using realistic test cases. The proposed FGMRES-D method is envisioned as a potential tool for improving the numerical solution when the direct preconditioning matrix is only partially effective in the FGMRES iteration. The development of the FGMRES-D method is motivated by the widespread adoption of direct solvers in finite-element methods. The proposed method is applicable in various contexts, including both stationary and time-dependent problems. The underlying assumption in the creation of the FGMRES-D method is that the linear system in question is solved exactly by the direct solver, with the exception of a small number of residual-only degrees of freedom. The term "small" is, in turn, defined as being proportional to the number of degrees of freedom in the system. The proposed method is shown to converge at a rate comparable to the standard FGMRES iteration. Accurate organ model registration is crucial for enhancing surgical outcomes and minimizing risks. However, the presence of noise in intraoperative imaging data can significantly impede the precision of registration results. This study focuses on developing a novel spatially-aware noise representation that facilitates efficient and accurate registration of liver tissues during laparoscopic surgery. The approach begins with analyzing noise patterns in intraoperative data and training multiple lightweight regression models to predict noise levels in previously unencountered areas. These predictions are then used to direct the registration process, which is otherwise constrained to minimize noise in newly mapped regions. The results of this study demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in accurately modeling organ surfaces and mitigating the influence of noise on registration outcomes, surpassing the performance of existing methods. The proposed framework also exhibits robust performance across diverse scenarios and datasets.

A self-supervised approach for estimating optical flow is introduced, with a proposed network that generates for forward and backward direction predictions. To encourage unique solutions, consistent flow was introduced as a constraint and established the basis for future improvements. However, significant challenges related to occlusions remain. To address this issue, the network can be further developed to accurately handle complex scenes with occlusions. The proposed framework's ability to manage occlusions was validated through an updated version of the Sintel dataset, with consistent self-supervised flow estimation results. The updated dataset includes precise segmentations, over 4600 training data samples, and refined ground truth flow mappings. The efficacy of the proposed approach is evident when compared to state-of-the-art self-supervised flow estimation techniques.

A novel spiking neural network (SNN) has been developed that serves as a general-purpose classifier on par with conventional artificial neural networks (ANNs), yet exhibits lower power consumption. This custom SNN consists of only 3 layers and incorporates dynamic threshold settings in its neurons to enhance performance. When tested on well-established MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets, our network demonstrated comparable, and in some cases superior, accuracy rates when operating at minimal power levels. In particular, on the MNIST dataset, our model achieves an accuracy rate of 99.18% on a small dataset and 97.19% on a limited dataset, both at a low memory usage. This performance comes as a result of our model's dynamic threshold feature, which enhances performance by multiplying inactive neurons' membrane potentials by zero. This reduces memory usage significantly. This proposal also includes a custom weight update algorithm and a method for handling output values, alongside simulation results and potential applications for this model.

Starting from a modified massive QCD model at finite temperature and chemical potential, we investigate the effects of a strong magnetic field on the quark mass terms and the interaction between quarks. We then derive the grand potential of the spin polarized quark gluon plasma in a strong magnetic field, and obtain the equation of state for strange quark matter in a strong magnetic field at finite temperature and chemical potential. We analyze the possible phases of strange quark matter in a strong magnetic field at finite temperature and chemical potential, and find that the quark gluon plasma phase can exist stably only within a narrow range of chemical potentials. We also calculate the masses of strange quark stars in a strong magnetic field at finite temperature and chemical potential, and investigate their properties including radius, mass, and compactness. We propose that strange quark stars could be detected through their characteristic periodic oscillations induced by the strong magnetic field.

A cubic graph is considered an E2F if all its 2-factors are even and there exists at least one 2-factor whose edges are non-adjacent. Cubic E2F graphs cannot contain the pattern "3-cycles only" as a subgraph and if they have more than one 2-factor, those 2-factors must be disjoint. This paper explores the even-factorability of a specific class of cubic graphs, called graphene-like cubic graphs, and provides an in-depth analysis of both planar and non-planar versions of this graph type.

This paper introduces a novel approach to system call filtering called
Timeloops, which enables applications in interpreted languages to effectively
prevent security breaches. Interpreted languages, which include popular choices
like PHP and Python, lack efficient system call filtering capabilities.
Consequently, existing solutions, while securing binary applications, cannot
be easily adapted for use with interpreted applications. To address this challenge,
Timeloops was developed with a primary purpose of securely implementing system
call filtering for applications in interpreted languages. This solution, which
is specifically designed to accommodate MySQL and Apache applications, employs
a unique hybrid technique that efficiently leverages the characteristics of
interpreted languages by combining two distinct methods of system call filtering.

This paper addresses the issue of efficiently tracking targets with limited sensor information by proposing a novel online anticipatory sensor scheduling and target tracking framework. The framework's main contribution is a method for processing target tracks that have gone unobserved for extended periods, incorporating a tree-based probabilistic representation to guide sensor placement, leading to a higher likelihood of detecting previously unseen targets. By deploying this strategy, the research demonstrates a notable reduction in the number of unobserved targets over time. Additionally, the proposed framework has the capability to adapt dynamically, allowing it to effectively manage changes in target movements and sensor capabilities, thereby enhancing its overall performance.

This research paper examines the observability properties of a population model that includes diffusion, demographic, and logistic components. By applying a single interior observation, we have discovered an inequality that can be used to determine an unobservable region. This observability information can be utilized to manage population decline or extinction within the unobservable region.

We've developed a probabilistic model that captures the essence of soccer dynamics and player behavior. By translating actions into a probability of shot attempt, our framework offers a data-driven comparison of various actions' reward potential. Our findings, supported by 10 years of Premier League data, reveal that committing a foul or causing the ball to go out often yields a higher reward than attempting a shot, especially in certain game scenarios. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that players tend to prioritize actions that result in ball possession over those that give the opposing team possession. Our probabilistic model also enables us to identify geographic preferences for different actions on the field.

A common issue in time-domain wavefield inversion arises from the significant increase in model parameters with time-domain data, leading to slow convergence and instability. To mitigate this challenge, this work develops an eigendecomposition-based approach for full waveform inversion utilizing time-domain wavefields. The proposed method extracts the most informative components of the time-domain wavefield and decouples them from less useful parts, thereby reducing the dimensionality of the problem. This approach facilitates faster convergence and improves robustness. The eigendecomposition-based technique is advantageous for time-domain data but can also be applied to frequency-domain data with minimal differences. Full waveform inversion with the eigendecomposition-based approach has been successfully tested and compared to conventional time-domain and frequency-domain techniques.

In an asymmetric noisy voter model, the tendency for individual agents to imitate neighbors can result in two distinct species of agents emerging over time, even when initial conditions are randomly arranged and completely symmetrical. This phenomenon was discovered by means of computer simulations in (Peltio et al., Phys Rev X 9, 041006 (2019)) and in the current study, we explain the underlying dynamics mathematically. When the probability of imitating a neighbor is greater than the probability of making a random choice, we find that two distinct populations with differing dynamics can develop through a non-equilibrium phase transition, which occurs when the speed at which agents adopt neighboring behaviors exceeds a certain threshold in comparison to the speed at which they adopt random behaviors. In addition, we demonstrate that this model is capable of producing multiple equilibrium states in the form of agent population segmentation, which can take various shapes, including domains, networks, or alignment with external fields. The asymmetric noisy voter model's behavior can be reinterpreted through the lens of an opinion dynamics model, where agents adopt the average opinion of their neighbors, and we show how this model generates different equilibrium states and phase transitions in the form of mean field solutions, which are supported by numerical results.

In a dual-everything-downlink (DED2D) system, a novel time-and-frequency information and energy transmission (TFIET) scheme is proposed to transfer both information and energy to users. This proposed method allocates separate frequency bands for information and energy transfer, leveraging the dual nature of the system to combine performance enhancement and energy harvesting. To optimize performance, two optimization problems are formulated to maximize the information rate and energy harvest simultaneously. To solve these problems, an hybrid decomposition method is suggested, involving initial feasible solution generation through an iterative algorithm, followed by enhanced dual update, and finally, the solution to the individual sub-problems through an interior point method. Simulations in a 2D scenario with multiple base station and mobile user configurations demonstrate improved information rate, reduced delay, and increased energy harvest compared to single-Everything schemes.

The pandemic-driven shift to remote working has caused an surge in requirements for automated experimental setup automation across various fields including psychology, medicine, and related research areas. As a result, there is a growing interest in leveraging artificial intelligence, specifically machine learning, to automate experiments and reduce dependencies on laboratory physical presence. However, the existing body of knowledge surrounding machine learning methods for automated experiments lacks a unified framework, causing difficulties in navigating effective approaches for specific research tasks. To address this challenge, this paper explores various machine learning methodologies for automated tasks such as subject recruitment, data cleaning, and experimental protocol execution, and also examines the use of augmented reality, a related field with potential applications in automated experiments. By reviewing 37 studies on machine learning for psychology and neuroscience experiments, this research provides a roadmap for researchers and practitioners on how to effectively combine machine learning, augmented reality, and other technologies to automate experiments and make psychology and neuroscience more accessible in the future.

The optimization of electrostatic phase plates is a complex task due to the interdependent effects of design parameters on electron probe size and current density. This study employs a genetic algorithm to explore various fill factors and pixel patterns of phase plates, resulting in the identification of several optimal configurations. The analysis indicates that increasing fill factor causes the electron probe to shrink in x-direction but grows in y-direction, whereas different pixel patterns exert distinct influences on the probe's shape. Specifically, a "checkerboard" pattern produces a probe with a small y-diameter and a large current density. Theoretical predictions are validated by simulations using the CASINO platform.

We investigate the orbital stability of solitary wave solutions in a one-dimensional anharmonic oscillator chain with weak anharmonic interactions. By extending the anharmonic oscillator's potential beyond the quadratic form, we examine how different types of nonlinearity influence the orbital stability of these solitary waves. Comparing different anharmonic potentials, we find that increasing anharmonicity can either promote or delay the collapse of these solitary waves, depending on their specific characteristics. Furthermore, we apply the energy landscape method to demonstrate that the orbital stability of these solutions is affected by the presence of anharmonicity, leading to the conclusion that weak anharmonic interactions do not disrupt the orbital stability of these solitary waves.

We establish an explicit relationship between the Galois group of a specific class of highly ramified finite non-abelian polynomial extensions of the rational numbers and the module structure of a particular ring additive theory. This connection stems from an in-depth examination of a renowned result by Kummer and Kronecker, who demonstrated that any finite non-abelian monic polynomial with distinct roots in the set of negative integers can be mapped to a cyclic extension with the property of having exactly one freely chosen rationally expressed root.

This letter describes a new search strategy for a neutral long-lived scalar particle, which can decay into two photons, using the CMS detector at the LHC. This particle is assumed to be produced individually and have a lifetime of 40 cm, allowing it to travel a significant distance before decaying. As a result, its optimal detection location within the CMS detector is identified as being near the endcaps, specifically at a distance of 11 meters from the interaction point. Following this, a protocol is established for identifying events featuring this particle, which involves setting minimum distances between the two-particle clusters formed by the decay and limiting the number of additional tracks within a certain radius. Furthermore, events are searched for in three different acceptance areas corresponding to different beam energies and with minimum energies of 30 EeV, 40 EeV, and 50 EeV. No evidence of this particle is found, and as such, upper limits on its production cross-section are established for different lifetime values. These limits provide constraints on theoretical models such as the one proposed by the "Monjola-Drell-Yan" scenario.

To understand how related words change in meaning over time, our proposed approach examines the differences in contextual distribution. However, we discover that simply considering the spread of contextual distributions might lead to misinterpretations due to variations in data quality. Consequently, our strategy for accurate analysis also considers the relation between words and their contextual basis, accounting for changes in contextual variance that result from data quality fluctuations. To demonstrate the significance of distinguishing data quality-induced shift from semantic shift, our approach shows that only by differentiating words with similar meanings from words with differing meanings, we can accurately capture the true meaning change of words over time. Moreover, our research reveals that common approaches to analyzing semantic change often produce misleading results that reflect data quality improvements rather than actual semantic evolution. To facilitate further research, our findings and proposed solutions are made available through an updated version of the SenseText dataset, which includes both the original text contexts and corresponding statistical descriptions required for controlling data quality-induced shift.

Re-examining the non-relativistic quasi-particle description for ultra-light dark matter, specifically axion-like dark matter, we re-derive the Lorentzian distribution of its mass spectrum. This is accomplished by re-interpreting the non-abelian dark matter model's scalar field equations in the non-relativistic limit. Our re-derived solution indicates that a very light particle can exhibit long-wavelength oscillations even when part of a dark matter field. In the process, we determine the re-scattering phase shifts that influence the quasi-particle spectrum, thereby establishing the conditions under which a minimal dark matter scenario could potentially be established or ruled out through upcoming, more sensitive experiments, including the Synergy Cosmic Ray Antenna and future, highly sensitive interferometric experiments with masses in the range of milligrams to kilograms.

Understanding how the retina's initial simple lens-covered surface transforms into the complex, multiple-layered structure we see in adult vertebrates is a longstanding and intricate problem. Retinogenesis research has been hindered by limited knowledge of early retinal development, specifically in higher vertebrates. To address this challenge, we used a combination of high-resolution imaging, computational modeling, and genetic analysis to study retinal development in zebrafish. By tracing individual retinal cells and mapping their ancestry, we discovered a distinct nuclear migration period characterized by randomly distributed cells with similar characteristics that gradually differentiate into distinct retinal layers. This information guided the development of a mathematical model, which revealed that the retinal layer's final shape results from interacting mechanical forces caused by the migration of these cells. This study reveals the crucial role of nuclear migration's random nature and the influence of a mechanism called active passive alignment on the formation of the adult vertebrate retina.

A critical challenge in compressive sensing is managing mutual coherence to achieve efficient recovery performance. Research indicates that, under certain conditions, the number of non-zero coefficients in a signal can be accurately estimated and tightly bound in relation to its $l_1$-norm. Building upon this finding and relevant research, we demonstrate that mutual coherence can be reduced through the use of a specific matrix, known as a D-optimal design matrix. Furthermore, we show that this reduction leads to improved recovery performance, specifically tight bounds on the $l_1$-norm of the residual in the case of linear measurements and on the number of measurements required for a specific signal class. These results represent novel contributions to the field of compressive sensing. A key application of signal reconstruction is also explored, in this case, to specifically address a problem related to multi-band image compression. The proposed approach is tested and shown to lead to better outcome when compared to existing methods.

We have used the linearized hydrodynamic theory to thoroughly explain driving forces and correlations in actively moving systems, specifically looking at the dynamics of randomly walking particles on lattices in dimensions 2 through 5. We have managed to overcome an inescapable time reversal symmetry by introducing a small imaginary component to time, which has a minimal impact on the scaled dimensions of our model.
