However, when considering the overall effects of CPM and SPM together, it becomes apparent that CPM generally exhibits stronger effects than SPM, with the degree of this superiority dependent on the relative strengths of the counterpropagating signals. In our research, we demonstrated that the intensity-dependent phase shifts associated with CPM and SPM have distinct nonlinear relationships. While these interactions result in the creation of optical shockwaves with broader spectral widths than those produced by self-phase modulation, the same effects can also lead to the generation of ultrashort pulses with much higher peak powers than those achieved with traditional self-phase modulation. Consequently, identifying cross-phase modulation, and specifically the dynamics governing CPM and SPM together, is crucial for accurately predicting and experimentally verifying nonlinear interactions in loop resonators.

We introduce a novel deep learning model that achieves significant improvements in upscaling very fine-scale data, as confirmed by our simulations of turbulent flow in channels at multiple Reynolds numbers including 5600, 56000, and 180000. By training the model on highly resolved simulations at a low Reynolds number and evaluating it at higher Reynolds numbers with coarse resolution simulations, we were able to compare its performance to traditional super-resolution methods. The results showed a notable reduction in turbulent kinetic energy and streamwise enstrophy in the model's predictions, indicating its ability to capture more detailed patterns in turbulence even when given minimal information. Furthermore, we found the model's effectiveness extended beyond our specific simulation, with a notable decrease in turbulent kinetic energy of approximately 10% across all Reynolds numbers studied. The fair agreement between the model's predictions and full resolution simulations, even at high Reynolds numbers, suggests its potential for scaling down highly resolved numerical simulations with large grid sizes.

We present a novel benchmark that assesses reinforcement learning methods through multiple, progressively difficult tasks, mirroring real-world challenges where problems don't necessarily present themselves in order of ease. To effectively evaluate reinforcement learning, we divide this benchmark into distinct stages, carefully managing the environment's complexity and measuring how learning is transferred across each stage. By controlled adjustments to curriculum design, we reveal how different reinforcement learning algorithms adapt to shifting levels of problem difficulty, providing valuable insights into performance improvements and areas for improvement. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that efficient reinforcement learning algorithms successfully leverage prior knowledge, exhibiting significant performance gains, while less efficient algorithms struggle with increased problem difficulty, often performing worse than random policy algorithms.

Process conformance checking analyzes observed data to identify how observed behaviors deviate from expected patterns and establishes a temporal framework known as DCR graphs to determine these deviations. Despite its effectiveness, this method primarily focuses on highlighting discrepancies and offers little insight into changes in processes over time, including innovations and natural evolution. To address this limitation, we propose a new framework called CCR graphs to explore changes in process behavior, building on top of the foundation laid by DCR graphs. This innovative framework provides multiple benefits, including the ability to distinguish causal relationships between process changes and provides feasible intervention strategies to improve process performance. To facilitate practical application, we develop a user-friendly tool that supports visual representation of CCR graphs, enabling users to explore and interact with the proposed solution in an intuitive manner.

The proposed study focuses on the characteristics of compactifications of moduli spaces for varieties of a specific type. We examine how these different compactifications coincide or diverge through a combination of analytical and geometric means. In particular, the study explores strategies for establishing the geometricity of compactifications, investigates how geometric and Hodge-theoretic compactifications converge or differ, and develops an approach for categorizing and distinguishing non-equivalent compactifications. The research is applied to a specific case study of moduli spaces for polarized irregular surfaces with specific attributes. The resulting analysis reveals that the components of the moduli space recognized through Hodge-theoretic means are distinct from those identified via geometric methods. The study ultimately demonstrates that the components recognized through Hodge-theoretic means or geometric means are always the same, even if they are not all mutually equivalent. The research is also extended to address a more general scenario involving surfaces with singularities and specific attributes in an algebraic family. The proposed approach is an extension of earlier research focused on surfaces with rational singularities and specific attributes. The study also recognizes previous contributions made by other researchers, including the results obtained by the proposed method and the components of the moduli space along with their characteristics.

We have discovered an intriguing pattern in observations of galaxies within the Leo cluster using the GALEX satellite, specifically in the near-ultraviolet (NUV). A significant shift in NUV-r color is observed, increasing substantially at around 10 to the power of 10.5 solar units of stellar mass. This mass threshold, where the color shift becomes more pronounced, corresponds to the expected point for low-mass galaxies transitioning from blue colors and is now noted as a feature worthy of further investigation. Furthermore, a notable rise in NUV-r color is seen in more massive galaxies above approximately 10 to the power of 11 solar units of mass, mirroring previous findings in other galaxy clusters. These findings are consistent with previous Leo cluster galaxy observations in the near-infrared and optical spectra, and the proposed explanation involves a lack of massive globular clusters in these galaxies.

Recently introduced few-shot learning methods achieve high accuracy in sentiment classification, however our analysis reveals that these results are largely achieved with language similarities rather than actual few-shot capabilities. To truly demonstrate the effectiveness of few-shot learning, our work moves beyond the usual English and Chinese classifications to explore sentiment analysis in Spanish. Utilizing only three examples in Spanish, our proposed FSL-OPT model successfully achieves significant improvements over the current best results in the SpanSent dataset. Furthermore, our model's ability to induce optimal feature transformations through the incorporation of optimal transport theory leads to enhanced performance across multiple Spanish datasets.

To address the critical challenge of allocating limited resources effectively, it's crucial to develop efficient methods for prioritizing patients with severe COVID-19 symptoms admitted to intensive care units (ICUs). Patient priority is a natural candidate for such a strategy, with better-priority patients receiving more comprehensive treatments. To facilitate efficient patient priority assignment, we propose a novel approach that employs multi-armed bandit reinforcement learning, taking into consideration the features associated with ICU admission, including specific COVID-19-related characteristics, to maximize patients' survival probabilities. Unlike previous studies focusing on single-arm experiments, our research leverages real-world data from the MIMIC-III database by modeling ICU priority as a multi-armed bandit problem, accounting for variability in treatment interventions and incorporating vital signs and laboratory test results to improve patient outcomes. To address data sparsity issues and promote responsible research, we will host the project on open-source platforms, providing reproducible results and contributing to the advancement of ICU priority management using machine learning methods.
The Giraud-KZ model comes into play when exploring the connection between the universal bundle functor and a specific kind of monad within the category of simplicial groups.

To mitigate the balanced negative proposal sampling issue encountered during Visual Relationship Detection, we analyze the VRD dataset and propose the Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling strategy. BNPS allocates model losses more effectively by dividing negative proposals into sub-categories and optimizing for the most challenging ones. Through thorough experimentation, we find that BNPS yields considerable improvements in model performance, with an overall mAP increase of 2.5% compared to the current state-of-the-art approach. To facilitate widespread adoption, BNPS is integrated into the popular Visual Relationship Detection dataset benchmark, alongside newly introduced evaluation metrics that account for dataset imbalance.

The merger fraction of galaxies must be monitored across billions of years to accurately understand galaxy formation. The detection of accretion streams is a reliable indicator of mergers, but their structure and impact on galaxies are not well understood, especially in the early stages of formation. Using the RAMSES-INTENSO super-large gravity hydrodynamic simulation of galaxy formation, a previously unreported dataset of accretion streams was mapped around a massive galaxy similar to our own at a time when the universe was three billion years old. This dataset was used to run an extensive set of N-body simulations, which in turn were compared to the actual distribution of accretion streams. As a result, the accretion streams were found to strongly impact the galaxies' mass distribution, causing them to adopt irregular shapes and driving the formation of bulges. Based on these findings, a parametric model was created to replicate the effects of accretion streams on galaxy formation, which in turn was used to demonstrate that the tight relationship between galaxies with dominant bulges and those without is influenced by the merger history of galaxies, specifically the presence of accretion streams.

A powerful X17 solar flare along with widespread solar activity occurred on November 7th, 2004, covering nearly an entire solar hemisphere. Unprecedented radio blackouts were observed at low altitudes and data from FLIP was used to determine the shock wave speed from the solar surface to the corona as approximately 460 km/s with an error of 40 km/s. Additionally, the energy released during the flare's instant phase was calculated to be around 1.74 x 10 to the power of 31 J with an associated error of 5 x 10 to the power of 29 J. This analysis also revealed that the solar neutron flux was 5.6 x 10 to the power of 4 neutrons per square centimeter per second with an error of 40% and the energy spectrum followed a power law with an index of 2.48 ± 0.03 with no evidence of a upper limit.

We conducted an exhaustive examination of KIC 9267654, an intriguing A-type main sequence, double-lined spectroscopic star noted for a distinctive and complex rotational profile. Our study involved analyzing all available data, incorporating a unusual eccentricity indicator from O'Connor et al., and considering possible explanations for the findings, including the presence of a tidal interaction, the star being in a temporary rotational state, or the presence of a stellar companion. We discovered that the rotational speeds of the star's components are significantly faster than expected and the spacing between their spectral lines varies over the orbital period. We believe that the most plausible explanation for this behavior is the presence of a close stellar companion with a relatively large orbit. If this is the case, we anticipate finding signs of the companion in through high-resolution imaging techniques, along with further clues about the star's evolutionary history, particularly regarding any mass transfer that may have occurred.

Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its potential for inflammation and misinformation dissemination. To combat the spread of fabricated information, it's essential to develop automatic methods for identifying false news articles. This study presents a novel deep learning-based framework, MetaFEND, designed to detect the authenticity of news articles. Leveraging a combined use of both convolutional neural networks and recurrent neural networks, the MetaFEND model achieves superior performance in fake news detection. In particular, it demonstrates a significant improvement over existing techniques, showcasing the effectiveness of this particular CNR-based approach in producing accurate results. To facilitate widespread adoption, the model is designed with accessibility in mind, featuring user-friendly training parameters that are easily replicable by other researchers. Moreover, the underlying architecture has been successfully applied to enhance the effectiveness of existing methods, including the renowned LSTMC and our proposed hybrid model, which combines both LSTMC and the new MetaFEND model.

This research paper examines a one-dimensional transport equation featuring periodic terrain with nonlocal flux, whose solutions, when started from odd initial data, eventually develop kinks within a finite time frame. Moreover, as time progresses to infinity, the solutions' intensities will either converge to a constant or fluctuate unpredictably. When the domain of definition has a finite extent, the solutions will also experience a sudden shift from one constant to the other within that domain, in addition to fluctuating within the infinite domain.

Quaternary Golay complementary array pair designs are highly sought after due to their versatility in generating complementary array pairs for various applications. However, creating these designs proves to be a challenging task. In this research, a new approach is taken to construct quaternary GCA pairs by utilizing a method that involves designing GCMs in a specific order, specifically with the use of balanced quaternary BCAs and GCAs. A key constraint of this approach is the requirement that the number of points in the design must be an power of 2, i.e. n = 2^m. As a result, this research leads to the successful creation of quaternary GCA pairs at the n = 32, 64, and 128 scale levels.

Researchers are seeking to create a solid-state quantum computer based on silicon physics, using silicon's natural properties to facilitate reliable and consistent quantum interactions. To achieve this goal, scientists are examining the silicon crystal's defects and how they behave under various conditions, as these defects can provide the necessary quantum bits, or qubits. By modeling the silicon crystal's defects, specifically focusing on the behavior of a single phosphorus atom in combination with nearby vacancies, researchers discovered that the exchange interaction, a key component of quantum computations, can vary significantly, up to 10-fold, depending on the vacancy's position in the crystal lattice. This discovery, published in the journal Physical Review X, also reveals that the exchange interaction's duration can be managed, or "tuned," by introducing substitutions, removing atoms, or altering the electron energy levels through electric fields. This research demonstrates that, with strategic planning, the exchange interaction's characteristics can be tailored to meet specific quantum requirements, potentially paving the way for reliable silicon quantum computers.

Recovering a system's underlying structure through probabilistic inference is crucial for understanding its functioning, especially in complex systems with multiple interconnected components. With dynamic systems, however, initial time series observations are more readily available than raw data, and can be leveraged to recover the underlying architecture. This paper introduces a novel neural process model called the Graph Neural State Space Network (GNSNN) that recovers a system's underlying structure and parameters from time series observations by incorporating a graph neural network within a state space model. This approach enables the recovery of both latent states and graph architecture through optimization of likelihood, and is demonstrated to be effective through experiments on both synthetic and real-world data, outperforming existing methods.

We introduce a concept called Homotopy Abstract Algebraic Geometry (HAAG), which serves as a theoretical framework for analyzing certain algebraic constructs within the context of stable homotopy theory. Specifically, HAAG provides a method for examining graded polynomial rings and their associated homotopy theorists via the application of homotopy theoretical invariants. These invariants can be viewed as elements in a abstract algebraic landscape, which can be compared to the foundational works of Serre, Quillen, and Mortensen on HAAG. Notably, our HAAG framework offers a unified analytical tool with far-reaching implications, as it is capable of interconnecting and extending the existing theories of HAAG.

A novel, adaptive region of interest (RoI) convolutional neural network (CNN) is proposed for medical image segmentation. The proposed system assigns a distinct subset of network weights to process each patient's data, enabling efficient cross-patient segmentation. In addition, a unique, shareable set of weights is allocated to process regions of interest (RoIs), facilitating efficient within-patient segmentation. The adaptive nature of the system is achieved through a proposed patch-based weighting update formula. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is demonstrated through a tumor segmentation experiment utilizing The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), which yields superior results when compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

GP 2, an iterative graph-based programming language, experienced significant performance issues due to inefficient memory management, leading to an 11-fold decrease in problem-solving efficiency. To address this challenge, GP 2's memory management system was revamped by introducing a new data structure called BigArray, which resulted in a substantial boost in solving problems, with some examples resolving them up to 7 times faster and others resolving them up to 11 times faster. Ultimately, the introduction of BigArray led to a 4-fold improvement in the overall performance of GP 2 programs.

Deep learning techniques have gained significant popularity in recent years, leading to a surge in publications utilizing these methods for various tasks. Our research tackles the challenge of image representation, aiming to develop a unified, layered deep belief network (LDBN) for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction. In this context, we define a layered deep belief network as a series of interconnected hidden layers, where each layer represents a feature from a specific, independent database. Our proposed LDBN framework consists of multiple, separately trained hidden layers that are later combined to derive a set of inclusive features. When no labels are provided, our method utilizes a stack of hidden layers to achieve unsupervised feature extraction. Conversely, with access to labels, our framework is adapted for supervised feature extraction through a single, fully connected layer. Our results demonstrate substantial improvements in classification accuracy across diverse datasets, including both unsupervised and supervised scenarios.

We develop an infinite family of topological graphs, labeled $\Theta_k$, consisting of $2+2k$ vertices in a hyperbolic plane. These graphs demonstrate a distinctive structure with a central edge connecting two mirror-image star-like components. What sets our construction apart from earlier, similar examples is the presence of a faithful action by a free group of rank 2 on each of the $\Theta_k$ graphs. This achievement is unprecedented in the realm of free groups acting on 2-dim topological graphs.

The development of regularization techniques such as Lasso and Elastic Net has significantly enhanced variable selection within the context of continuous or categorical data. Building on these advancements, the Group Lasso algorithm extends such constraints to create groups of variables that can potentially be eliminated during the optimization process. In the course of researching Group Lasso, an improved algorithm was discovered that refines existing methods by utilizing an interior point method and augmentative Lagrangian multipliers to facilitate solution finding. Theoretical and empirical evidence confirms that this novel algorithm yields an optimal solution along with an estimate of the sparse vector. The interior point method's efficiency is further demonstrated through a series of timely and complex experiments involving realistic datasets and artificial problems.

Recently introduced TADAM and CoOp methods, which leverage knowledge graphs for visual recognition tasks, used model pre-training on factual triples from a general knowledge base. In comparison to these methods, our findings show that models pre-trained on factual information perform significantly worse than those trained on traditional text-based data for question-answering tasks. Nonetheless, knowledge graph pre-training does offer certain benefits, particularly in the case of questions whose answers are included in the underlying knowledge base, such as Wikidata. When working with incomplete knowledge bases, our proposed framework, Knowledge Augmented Model (KAM), is able to enhance the pre-trained model through a data augmentation strategy that intentionally transforms regular triples into inconsistent ones, leading to a 12% improvement in our evaluation.

This work introduces a novel algorithm that reinterprets the concept of line joins, redefining their appearance as dynamic paths as opposed to fixed, pre-drawn strokes. By doing so, a range of limitations associated with traditional line join rendering are addressed. Specifically, the proposed solution mitigates the issues related to fan-shaped line joins, eliminating the need for the abrupt termination of lines and join components, thereby creating a more organic and cohesive visual effect. To achieve this, the algorithm employs a tracking mechanism to monitor the movement of curves and curve segments, ensuring that even as curves shift, the apparent origin of the join remains visible, producing a more natural-looking and engaging graphical experience.

In this work, a novel speech enhancement technique is presented that leverages a unique Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) framework. This system divides the frequency domain into distinct subsets, employing different convolution and recurrent components for each subset. By doing so, it independently improves the time-domain signals corresponding to each frequency subset, resulting in an improved Denoising Autoencoder. The proposed DPCRN structure's effectiveness is demonstrated through speech enhancement, leading to notable gains in both the SEGB and FR-SNR metrics when compared to existing time and frequency domain approaches.

We employ a two-fluid model to simulate small but significant temperature gradients in low-contrast fluids and conduct a linear stability analysis of a statically stable, slowly heated fluid in a confined environment. The results of the analysis yield specific predictions for the behavior of heat flux and the location of the onset of convection, which align with observations from experiments featuring significant temperature differences. The predicted relationship between the size of the thermal driving force and the rate of heat transfer also matches the findings from such experiments, which indicate a nonlinear relationship governed by an power law of approximately two and a half. The predicted relationship between the size of the thermal driving force and the rate of heat flux that we obtain through theoretical means is in agreement with the results from earlier numerical simulations featuring highly contrasting fluids, which also employed a two-fluid model. The predicted reduction in the heat flux threshold in a rotating system is in agreement with the findings from earlier experiments and numerical simulations, which used a single-fluid model. The use of a two-fluid model also allows us to identify the causes of these effects on the heat flux threshold, which include the effects of thermal diffusion, the reduction of the heat flux threshold near the onset of convection in a rotating system due to the Taylor-Proudman balance, and the effects of boundary conditions in confined systems.

We investigate a parameterized family of holonomic phases driven dynamically, whose members involve a cavity interacting with multiple atoms. The assumption that an uncorrelated atom is present causes it to contribute insignificantly to the dynamics, leading to a reduced version that can be solved exactly. This version exhibits a singular phenomenon where the entanglement between the cavity and the remaining atoms suddenly vanishes, yet eventually recovers as a nonclassical resource for generating multipartite entanglement among the atoms. By contrast, the full version exhibits a more complex behavior resulting in a extensive number of parameter settings with non-orthogonal holonomic phases, yet ultimately producing a vast amount of multipartite entanglement efficiently.

Recently, LSTM-based sentiment analysis has been successfully applied, and
our team built upon this work. In our proposed method, we used LSTM and
C-LSTM networks to categorize the sentiment of tweets. Our key contribution
involves combining the capabilities of both network types to achieve enhanced
performance. We used a unique fusion strategy to combine their output and
our team demonstrated improved results using this combined model. We used
publicly available datasets and our findings showed that the proposed C-LSTM
based model delivered the best outcomes when compared to other state-of-the-art
techniques.

Within the context of non-linear electrodynamics and non-linear Yang-Mills (YM) theory, an approximate analysis reveals that the YM charge parameter affects the radius of the shadow and the thermal profile of black holes. By considering non-rotating and charged de Sitter black hole as an example, we numerically investigate the impact of non-linear YM theory on shadow geometry and temperature distribution. The simulation shows that the distortion of the shadow becomes more pronounced with increasing YM charge, while the temperature gradient near the event horizon also changes with the YM charge. These findings support previous conjectures made under approximate analysis.

We apply the novel approach of introducing a 4d Wigner function based on the Dirac formalism to describe a two-level optical cavity system. This allows us to identify specific nonclassical phenomena, such as entanglement dynamics, by examining distinct features in corresponding optical tomograms. Using a generic two-level atom in contact with a single-mode cavity and subject to a classical driving field, we have been able to derive a comprehensive analytical expression for the 4d Wigner function and subsequent optical tomograms for all time points. These results can be compared to their classical counterparts obtained through the Henneberger equivalent picture. By employing the entanglement monotonic criterion, we can also graphically present the development of entanglement over time. Furthermore, we visually demonstrate the distinct differences in associated phase space structures, Wigner function distributions, and optical tomograms in various scenarios.

Immersive videos are increasingly found on social media and online platforms, and predicting viewer attention is crucial for enhancing user experience. Unlike regular videos, immersive videos include subtitles that can aid in attention forecasting by providing contextual information. In light of this, our proposed approach aims to enhance viewport prediction models by incorporating subtitles as additional input. The subtitles are first pre-trained to extract features, which are then used in a minority-class oversampling technique to enhance the effectiveness of attention prediction. Furthermore, our approach includes a design for displaying subtitles during free-viewing sessions to improve viewport prediction accuracy. The results of our experiments indicate significant improvements in viewport prediction accuracy when using subtitles, with gains of over 20% in certain cases. The proposed approach can be integrated into existing viewport prediction models, and our findings demonstrate the value of considering subtitles in attention forecasting.

Our fresh interpretation employs a novel type of approximate physical exotic pure exotic orbital (PEPO) block to reinterpret the gauge-gravity duality for finite-sized systems, specifically focusing on finite temperature and time evolution. We deviate from standard PEPO structure by introducing an additional degree of freedom to account for thermal fluctuations and time-dependent behavior. The modified PEPOs come with a higher bond dimension that increases proportionally to the square of the system's size, a necessary compromise that allows for accurate approximation of thermal states and time evolution. We further analyze the relationship between the PEPO's bond dimension and the tolerance for approximation, discovering it adheres to a universal law that can be used to guide the choice of bond dimension for a given application.

We combine two advanced analytic techniques to achieve a higher level of understanding in the study of a particular nonlinear equation. Specifically, we utilize a novel application of Taylor series expansion and canonical surfaces to analyze and solve the problem of energy concentration mentioned in [Bourgain, 2004]. This research builds upon the foundations established in [Bourgain, 2004], [Colliander et al., 2003], and [Tao, 2004]. By integrating these methodologies with the concepts developed in [Tao, 2006], we significantly enhance the decoupling distance, ultimately obtaining a combined result that can be applied to the analysis of the Klein-Gordon equation. This achievement surpasses the previous records set in [Hou, 2012] and [Bui, 2013] by means of different analyses. This research is part of an ongoing project initially presented in an earlier format at the 2019 AMS MathFest.

The distribution of gluons within protons is crucial for understanding various particle interactions and certain fundamental processes. By combining distinct deep inelastic scattering (DIS) and lattice Monte Carlo methods, researchers have made notable progress in mapping this distribution, known as the gluon density. This study builds upon those findings and provides a more precise estimate of the gluon density within the low to intermediate x range, incorporating both lattice lattice QCD data and a range of existing deep inelastic scattering experiments. The resulting distribution includes both a deterministic component and an inherent uncertainty, which is driven by the inherent ambiguities in the deep inelastic scattering data used as inputs. This uncertainty is then represented through a stochastic distribution, which is subsequently used to make predictions for various processes, such as prompt photon and vector meson production in protons. The findings regarding the gluon density also imply a revised estimate of the strong coupling constant, which is found to be more precise than previously reported. The expanded knowledge of the gluon density does, however, slightly reduce the range of possible values for the strong coupling constant.

Research on magnetophotonic crystals has yielded various fascinating phenomena when surface plasmons and a Rayleigh anomaly interact. By designing a specific grating on a magnetophotonic crystal surface, researchers have interfered surface plasmon and Rayleigh anomaly modes to enhance magneto-optical effects. This study theoretically examines the interference between these modes and surface plasmon/Rayleigh anomaly pairs with the same wavelength but different propagation directions. The results show that stopping the propagation of surface plasmon/Rayleigh anomaly at a specific point through geometric phase can lead to an increase in the amplitude of the magnetic field by up to 30 times, with a significant shift in the spectral feature from the original position. This shift becomes more pronounced with increasing free electron surface plasma resonance, as the shift itself also increases with a maximum of 30 nm. Additionally, increasing the width of the grating can lead to an increase in the amplitude of the magnetic field as well as a broader spectral feature.

The quest for efficient neural network training continues, with knowledge distillation emerging as a reliable standard.
However, standard knowledge distillation relies on access to training data, limiting its effectiveness.
In contrast, decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, involving only model predictions, has been successfully employed.
Yet, despite its advantages, DB3 knowledge transfer differs from the original, leading to suboptimal results.
To address this, we introduce semi-supervised DB3, leveraging both limited labeled data and model predictions.
In particular, we develop a framework where DB3 knowledge transfer occurs in two stages.
Initially, we use model predictions to train a low-cost density estimator, which subsequently informs a full knowledge distillation process using only a limited amount of labeled data.
As we will demonstrate, this two-stage approach significantly improves the efficiency of DB3 knowledge transfer.

Our detailed investigation into the multiple decay pathways of the B- s → K- ∗0γ system has yielded several key findings. By examining approximately 37 million B s → K ∗0γ events, we have made precise determinations of various branching fractions and charge ratios associated with this decay process. Notably, our research has enabled us to undertake simultaneous fits for the two distinct modes of K ∗0 decay (K- π+ and K- π-), allowing us to provide the first-ever estimates for the branching fractions of these K ∗0 decay modes in B s decays into photon radiation. Our branching fraction calculations for these K ∗0 decay modes in B s decays are 1.06 ± 0.09 (stat.) ± 0.06 (syst.)% for K- π+ and 0.78 ± 0.08 (stat.) ± 0.05 (syst.)% for K- π-, respectively. Furthermore, our study has produced updated estimates for the branching fractions of the B s → K- γ and φγ decay processes, with results of 4.6 ± 0.4 (stat.) ± 0.3 (syst.) × 10−5 for the former and 1.00 ± 0.15 (stat.) ± 0.09 (syst.) × 10−5 for the latter, with no evidence found for these processes in particle antip

Let's consider a Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ and a representation $\mathfrak{g}$-module $\mathfrak{n}$. For a module $\mathfrak{n}$ that is multiplicity free under the adjoint action of $\mathfrak{g}$, we explore how its composition factor lattice looks like compared to a given set of roots $\Phi$. If $\mathfrak{g}$ has a root system similar to one of type $A$, $D$, or $B$, and if we know the weights and corresponding irreducible components of $\mathfrak{n}$, then we can completely reconstruct the lattice of composition factors of $\mathfrak{n}$. However, for a Lie algebra of type $C$ or $E$, determining the composition factor lattice of a multiplicity free module is more complex and requires additional information.

Our novel approach, Co-Imitation Learning, enables the acquisition of new skills without requiring expert guidance. In contrast to traditional imitation learning methods that necessitate access to perfect demonstrations, Co-Imitation Learning allows for the creation of desirable behaviors through feedback related to desired outcomes, not precise action mappings. This more realistic framework leverages reinforcement learning to identify optimal actions in new situations and incorporates feedback about desired outcomes through a value-based method. Our name-to-action mapping technique utilizes both value function and policy to determine the most suitable actions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by developing two Co-Imitation Learning systems: one capable of imitating human instructions and another capable of imitating human feedback in game-like scenarios. Our results show that Co-Imitation Learning surpasses traditional imitation learning methods.

We analyze the performance of a maximum-likelihood (ML) decoder under a specific channel condition where the transmitter and receiver share a common language. This assessment is carried out in a scenario where data is transmitted incrementally, beginning with an unreliable initial transmission. The goal is to compare the accuracy of a ML decoder when it makes decisions based on different biased estimates from the initial transmission. The primary performance metric examined is the probability of the decoder producing incorrect outcomes. The performance of the ML decoder is represented by its error probability, which is expressed as an expected value of a cumulative distribution function (CDF) obtained from the underlying channel. The subsequent investigation involves a cutoff rate-based assessment and ultimately leads to a threshold-based representation of the decoder's error probability. The results reveal that the probability of the decoder making an error can be represented as a beta-regularized CDF, which arises due to the nature of the binary symmetric channel. The final analysis includes an in-depth numerical example that demonstrates the performance of the ML decoder under a specific error probability threshold and a predetermined bias, in addition to highlighting the significance of a particular bias value known as the cutoff rate.

This paper explores the utilization of reinforcement learning post-editing for improved performance in machine translation. Rather than focusing solely on optimizing the policy space, our research reveals that leveraging reinforcement learning with an optimized action space yields significantly better results. To achieve this, we developed a novel reinforcement learning framework that initially obtains a high-quality policy and subsequently refines the action space, resulting in significant improvements in performance. Furthermore, our work introduces a new reinforcement learning objective that considers the inter-gram level and contributes a data-driven approach to evaluating post-editing quality. The results of our experiments, conducted on three distinct language pairs and using three different base models, consistently show that optimized action spaces lead to performance gains in machine translation.

Within the quantum harmonic oscillator framework, we've developed a novel non-local information flow model for an open system in relation to its surroundings. This system, with two parts, represents a quantum entity that has become separated into two non-individually accessible components. It interacts with multiple electromagnetic modes and has two degrees of freedom. We've derived two distinct information flow dynamics based on two different types of interactions: a bidirectional flow dynamic where information flows freely in both directions, and a reversible flow dynamic where information flows in only one direction but can be reversed. These information flow dynamics result in distinct Wigner function distributions, offering a feasible scenario for investigating reversible and irreversible information flow through explicit calculations and comparisons.

In the context of Euclidean space, we have identified new recurrent operators that can be applied to biharmonic hypersurfaces, potentially leading to a more comprehensive classification than previous work. Specifically, we have discovered that biharmonic hypersurfaces with specific symmetries or curvature properties can be classified as minimal surfaces when they meet particular area or volume criteria. This research builds upon the existing framework for biharmonic hypersurfaces and provides new insights into both minimal and biharmonic geometry.

We introduce the concept of p/q-automata for subsets of natural numbers represented in rational form (N_p/q) and extend this idea to higher dimensions (N_p/q)^d. This leads to the definition of p/q-recognisable subsets in (N_p/q)^d and we demonstrate that these subsets correspond to specific rational expressions, thereby establishing the equivalence to p/q-languages. Furthermore, we identify the boundaries of (N_p/q)^d and show that within these boundaries, any subset of (N_p/q)^d that is p/q-recognisable also has a non-deterministic equivalent representation.

This paper introduces an original formal framework for specifying and
analyzing concurrency control mechanisms in database systems using
temporal logic. We apply this framework to a comprehensive examination of
snapshot isolation variants and their corresponding implementations in various
database systems, including MongoDB's WiT, Replicasa, and ShardedCluster.
We then examine the consistency guarantees provided by these systems and
identify gaps in their implementations. Furthermore, we demonstrate how using
extended concurrency control protocols, such as multi-granularity locking, can
enhance the snapshot isolation variants offered by these systems.

Preon states are represented as signed, weighted combinations of Dyck paths that satisfy a specific condition when mapped to nonnegative integers. A particular kind of Dyck path, known as a Gessel lattice path, is used to define these preon states. Building on the earlier work of Melham, we develop a positive formulation for (x_1,...,x_n)-colorings of rooted trees in terms of their root structures. This enables us to demonstrate that every preon state corresponds to a nonnegative integer combination of Gessel lattice paths that match its generating function. Conversely, we can also derive the (x_1,...,x_n)-coloring generating function from its corresponding preon state. As an additional contribution, we show that a specific subset of these preon states results in weighted versions of the chromatic symmetric functions, expressed as e-positive combinations of elementary symmetric polynomials.

We studied a 2D lattice that consists of interconnected equilateral triangles, using a classical Ising model to explore its magnetic properties. By focusing on the unique interactions between the spins at the vertices of the triangles (specifically, the non-bonded interactions), we found that they cause the hysteresis loop of the system to change shape in a distinct way. The interactions cause the magnetic field to switch the spins more slowly at the corners of the triangles, creating sharp bends in the hysteresis loop that point towards those corners. As the temperature increases, the loop becomes more circular, but its shape can be identified by looking at the proportions of the angles. The unique shape of the loop can potentially serve as an indicator of the presence of triangular geometry in magnetic hysteresis, and could be used to identify triangles in complex networks.

We studied a vast collection of 3463 NASA-cleaned-up comet trajectories from the JPL Small Body Data Center, focusing on 728 comets that entered the solar system with velocities indicating they originated from stellar-type, interstellar spaces. Our analysis revealed a notable disparity in energy levels required for escape from the solar system at distances near Earth's orbit, ranging from 0.8 to 1.2 times the energy needed for escape from the current solar state, when considering their actual trajectories and orientations. In contrast, most comets that rapidly left the solar system had significantly lower energy requirements, with distributions shifted towards smaller energies than those needed for escape from the observed solar state at distances within Earth's orbit. This implies that many of these comets could have originated from a solar system with a weaker gravitational pull, possibly one in its final stages of mass loss.

In the realm of affective language recognition, models typically train on a single data set within a particular language. Yet, real-world applications necessitate a more adaptable approach, one that can effectively identify emotions across diverse data sets and languages. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel, multi-task deep learning framework called MT-EDL, designed to simultaneously process multiple data sets and languages. This framework leverages a shared, high-level representation, thereby increasing efficiency and effectiveness. Through theoretical analysis and experimental results, we demonstrate that MT-EDL achieves significant improvements in emotion recognition accuracy across different languages and data sets. Specifically, our experiments show that MT-EDL exhibits enhanced performance in recognition tasks spanning Chinese, English, and Spanish, and multiple data sets in each language.

When a powerful shock wave with a high adiabatic index passes through a polymer model of a granular medium, unusual behavior is observed near the origin. Unlike regular shocks that smooth out over time as the number of collisions increases, this shock initially strengthens and then breaks apart, creating multiple shocks. This peculiar phenomenon only occurs when the shock's strength exceeds a certain threshold, which depends on the properties of the granular material. In a state of mechanical equilibrium, the effects of the shock wave persist, as it leaves behind a pattern of alternating dense and sparse regions of material. For a granular material with a uniform initial distribution of particle sizes, the effects of the shock wave cause small particles to become concentrated in dense areas, while larger particles are found in areas of lower density. In a non-uniform distribution, the effects of the shock wave are more pronounced, as it can change the size distribution of particles in certain areas. Similar behavior is observed in models of elastic and plastic materials under stress, but only in areas near the origin. Farther away from the origin, multiple shocks break apart into many smaller shocks.

The decay rate distributions of heavy quarks can be categorized using two theoretical frameworks: the CLN format, which involves polynomial expressions, and the BGL format, characterized by fractional expansions. By correlating these frameworks, we have derived novel representations for the $\bar{B}_s\rightarrow \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B\rightarrow K^*\gamma$ decay rates. These representations offer distinct benefits over existing formulations, with the BGL format providing a transparent demonstration of the impact of form factor effects on $B\rightarrow K^*\gamma$ decay. Additionally, we have identified an equation that relates the BGL format to the CLN format, which can be further modified to accommodate the impact of electroweak corrections on $\bar{B}_s\rightarrow \mu^+\mu^-$ decay.

A One-Dimensional Supersymmetric (1D SUSY) quantum mechanism is employed to generate a family of precisely defined potentials from the fundamental harmonic oscillator. The resulting potentials, which exhibit quantum non-singularity, are found to be part of a polynomial Heisenberg algebra. The algebraic structure of 1D SUSY quantum mechanics leads to the creation of mirror potentials in a "partner" sector, for each generated potential. The investigation of both the original and mirror potentials reveals that they all participate in a larger set of potentials that are interconnected and form a closed chain, with each being the mirror of the other in a rotating sequence. The achievable mirror potentials can be viewed as created through successive applications of a proposed "mirror generator" operator, whose action on the initial harmonic oscillator results in the most physically diverse mirror potential. The interconnection among the potentials, as demonstrated through explicit examples, can be expressed in a variety of rotational transformation matrices, including classical, quantum, and semi-classical configurations. The research offers a comprehensive understanding of the interlinked potentials, as well as their respective quantum spectra, which are exhibited in detailed comparisons of energy pattern transformations.

A nonlinear time-series analysis technique is introduced, based on a coupled complex network, to investigate the local dynamics of a system through a linearized approach. By applying this method to the study of the Lorenz system's chaotic behavior, we were able to reconstruct the underlying statistics that control its exponential growth pattern for different parameter values. This reconstruction is further shown to be controllable through a coupled network, offering practical insights into the erratic movements observed in the Lorenz system.

Within the non-abelian thermal quantum field theory, we examine the impact of a proposed non-abelian aether term, described by a linear combination of specific commutators, on the Casimir energy and the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law for a specific non-abelian massive scalar field in $(1+1)$-dimensional space. The investigation involves analyzing the impact of this aether term on the Casimir energy and the non-abelian temperature dependence of the free energy. The results indicate that the aether term causes a shift in the non-abelian temperature, leading to the inhibition of temperature-dependent interactions. The Casimir energy can be represented as a sum of the zero-point energy and the aether term, which contributes a positive amount to the energy. The aether term also causes the inhibition of the spontaneous symmetry breaking, with the scalar field's self-coupling being a required condition for this phenomenon.

This study introduces an integrated approach that speeds up highly accurate hedge liquidity cost predictions under stochastic process frameworks. The method involves deriving a novel integration formula that efficiently calculates hedge liquidity costs before hedging via the solution to a nonlinear Bellman equation, assembled from individual flow components. The formula outperforms existing, faster methods, yielding results comparable to Monte Carlo simulation for fair value predictions. The research also develops a nonlinear control-based method for calculating expected hedge liquidity costs, demonstrating improved performance compared to conventional Monte Carlo simulation, with a significant reduction in computation time. The analysis is demonstrated using a put option valuation scenario, showing that the integrated approach provides accurate results quickly.

The concept of "social opportunity" has been used to describe fundamental chances that significantly influence an individual's socioeconomic status. This study explores the idea that allocated social opportunities, in turn, depend on the socioeconomic status of previous generations. To examine this dynamic relationship, we use a stochastic process to model the interactions between socioeconomic status and social opportunities. The resulting distribution of socioeconomic status can be seen as a generalized Pareto distribution. To test the validity of these models, we use European data on social mobility. The results show that the observed social mobility patterns are likely the result of a specific, underlying mechanism that prioritizes individuals with higher socioeconomic status in the allocation of opportunities. This finding indicates that the allocation of opportunities often favors those who are already more fortunate, leading to increased inequality across generations. To manage inequality effectively, we must consider policy interventions that have a lasting impact on the allocation of opportunities and, by extension, on future socioeconomic status.

In particle accelerators, the interaction between opposing beams and their identical orbits influences the performance and can be measured by calculating the beam-beam closed orbit differences. Accurate beta function measurement from closed orbits can be beneficial, especially in machines like the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) with complex physics. This paper discusses how beam beam interactions affect the closed orbit, specifically the impact of nonlinear effects which become prominent at high energy circulation in the LHC. It is demonstrated how beta star, resulting from nonlinear interactions at high energy circulation, can be determined from closed orbit measurements along with other key parameters like the longitudinal closure, cross-talk, and beam size at high energy circulation. This research was conducted using simulated data from the Linac to Irresistible Bunch Interactions program and real data from closed orbit measurements in the SPS and LHC.

We introduce a novel distributed optimization framework where cooperation is necessary to tackle challenging tasks, incorporating both collaborative and individual projects for agent efficiency. In this context, we develop two primary algorithms to solve distributed optimization problems while managing communication with other agents. Firstly, we create the DOPC algorithm, which minimizes the impact of malicious agents that deliberately disrupt communication by sending misleading information. The DOPC algorithm is shown to efficiently complete both shared and individual projects within specified timeframes. Secondly, we develop the FEDC algorithm, which handles the influence of malicious agents that intentionally disrupt communication by sending incorrect updates. The FEDC algorithm is found to effectively complete individual projects while managing the spread of incorrect information related to the shared project. Both algorithms are proven to be robust in environments with both non-malicious and malicious agents.

The SimInstrument suite, designed to mimic instrumental effects for
cosmological research and future instrument development, has undergone
significant expansions in our previous work. This note highlights the
latest additions to SimInstrument, focusing on aspects that characterize
its uniqueness within the broader context of instrumental simulation tools.

Future cosmological experiments will push the limits of current
technologies to the forefront, and it is essential to test and evaluate
existing instruments and technology in a controlled, simulated
environment. Such simulation can be beneficial for several purposes,
including real-time data processing, the development and testing of
dataanalysis algorithms, and for feeding simulated signals into the
analysis of theoretical models. Although instrumental simulation can be
complex, with various effects influencing the final outcome, it is
feasible to keep the focus narrow and manageable for specific
cosmological studies. Nonetheless, a versatile simulation instrument
with wide applicability would offer even greater benefits, and for
this purpose, we present SimInstrument, a dedicated suite designed
to mimic instrumental effects on multi-frequency far-IR to millimeter-wave
observations, including both optical properties of instruments
and signal processing algorithms. This package is particularly
tailored to facilitate easy integration with existing cosmological
simulations and Monte Carlo Markov Chain (MCMC) chains, and we
demonstrate the utility of SimInstrument by applying it to a linear
polarization instrument in a Bayesian analysis of polarized cosmic
microwave background.

This study delves into the analysis of BART's performance in two linguistic manipulation tasks: word ordering and partial tree linearization. Initially, BART was assessed in a task where it had to rearrange randomly selected words from a sentence into their correct order. The results revealed that BART excelled in this task, achieving a score of 96.3%. To gain a deeper understanding of BART's capabilities, the researchers also tested it in a related task called partial tree linearization, where they provided BART with the linearized form of some words in a sentence and asked it to determine the correct order for the remaining words. In this case, BART's performance was measured at 83.6%. It's worth noting that both of these tasks post-date BART's training data and involve sentences that are grammatically correct. To further challenge BART, the researchers created a new word ordering task called Fill-in-the-Blank, where they removed various words from sentences and asked BART to replace them with the correct words. Interestingly, when evaluating BART in this task, the researchers found that it performed significantly worse, with a score of 42.5%. This suggests that while BART possesses a high level of grammatical knowledge, it requires additional training in sentence structure and grammar through supervised learning.

Recently introduced deepfake detection networks, which employ shared parameters across domains, have shown a significant improvement in accuracy. Building upon this progress, our proposed DeepDomainNet harnesses inter-domain connections to further boost performance. We conceptualize a multi-domain trick-injection module, which leverages connection weights to enhance inter-domain sharing, and employ this module to enhance existing detected techniques. Through the introduction of cross-stitch connections in sharing strategies, our results indicate a notable reduction in errors achieved on the FaceForenisc++ dataset, specifically in the low-resolution image category, while also demonstrating comparable performance on high-resolution images when compared to the current standard. Our evaluation across the adult human video dataset, Deepfake Detection Dataset, reveals improved performance over multiple baselines, with error rates as low as 0.06 and 0.08 for low and high-resolution images respectively.

We extend the concept of angle functions to areas with negative curvature and points of non-positive intrinsic diameter. This expanded definition enables us to address two significant problems. Firstly, it is now possible to determine if a graph that is locally infinite can be conformally embedded within the plane based on angle function information alone. Secondly, we provide a more general proof that an infinite planar graph can be conformally embedded in the hyperbolic plane using the same method used in Bilardo's proof for a specific class of graphs.

We derive a novel inequality relating key measures to the distribution of isomorphism classes of orders in a family of number fields. Under certain assumptions, this can be transformed into a non-trivial upper bound for the number of isomorphism classes within the given family. Combining this result with estimates from previous research, we obtain an improved estimate for the number of isomorphism classes of maximal orders in a given family of quadratic fields.

We establish a fundamental basis $\bar{\Theta}$ for the quantum group $U_q(\mathfrak{g})$, and prove that it possesses distinct characteristics under the influence of Lusztig's braid group action and Dynkin automorphisms $\sigma$ and $\tau$. These distinct properties result in $\bar{\Theta}$ being equivalent to a subset of $\Theta$ with specific characteristics, and this subset can be identified as the $\tau$-orbits within $\Theta$. Consequently, the $\tau$-orbits within $\Theta$ are found to comprise a basis for the quotient space $U_q(\mathfrak{g}) / \langle \sigma \rangle$.

A recent example of a highly successful survivalism-based cryptocurrency scheme known as Forsage has gathered significant global attention, with participants from over 160 countries and revenues exceeding $300 million. In order to examine the financial stability of this scheme and its impact on users, our research acquired an in-depth financial dataset containing 46,000 individual user records. By analyzing these records, our findings reveal that nearly 99% of Forsage users suffer financial losses and the majority of revenues are concentrated among a small group of top participants. Furthermore, our research reveals that Forsage's financial structure allows it to maintain a stable cash flow and infrastructure, with over $20 million allocated for promotional purposes and operational expenses. Nonetheless, the long-term sustainability of this scheme remains uncertain and unlikely due to the inevitable decline in new user recruitment and resulting cash flow.

The Milky Way's vast bulge is home to a limited number of stellar clusters.  An inventory of the galaxy's cluster population, particularly in its ancient northern hemisphere, is lacking.  We conducted a thorough survey of this region, using data from the VISTA survey of the Milky Way, to discover new clusters and gain a deeper understanding of the galaxy's cluster population in this area.  After conducting a comprehensive analysis of the survey data, we identified 14 potential globular cluster candidates that were then evaluated using high-resolution images from the Hubble Space Telescope.  Unfortunately, only one of these candidates could be confirmed as a genuine globular cluster.  The newly confirmed cluster, which we've designated as VVV-GC194, appears as a small, densely packed group of ancient stars with a well-defined central black hole.  Based on this discovery, we created detailed, three-dimensional models of the cluster and its surrounding field stars, allowing us to draw key conclusions about the cluster's composition, distance, and movement within the galaxy. For a class of discrete systems where a single kind of tensor serves as a correctable erasure decoding, we develop a novel Gaussian average action principle. This principle leads to a single-type tensor network equation and subsequently a family of matrix product density operator equations. These equations can be viewed as a broad generalization of the typical boundary condition scenario. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the single-type tensor network equation can be reduced to obtain the familiar matrix product state (MPS) equations under the assumption of minimal entropy. The resulting MPS equation can be seen as a type of entanglement threshold theory. The associated gap matrix also represents the error correction cost for each individual site. The combination of these findings and the inherent unitary time-reversal symmetry of the systems under consideration enables the derivation of the entanglement threshold from a single-type tensor network perspective. The ensuing entanglement spectrum analysis can be performed without assuming the sector of minimal entropy, in contrast to previous studies. The proposed approach can be applied to investigate the dynamics of systems where the systems' parameters are subject to random fluctuations caused by the introduction of disorder. The resulting entanglement spectrum indicates that the systems' entanglement will eventually become delocalized and exhibit power-law behavior as the systems' parameters undergo a random phase transition.

By integrating process and prediction data, our proposed framework provides a way to capture performance fluctuations throughout a complex business process. This process, which involves multiple stages, can be represented by a directed acyclic graph, allowing us to identify relationships between prediction models and their corresponding stages. We offer two novel metrics to assess model performance in a comparative context, accounting for both absolute scoring and relative staging. This facilitates stage-specific model performance comparisons, enabling us to determine if performance differences are statistically significant. We further develop an approach to mine rule-based patterns from model performance data, factoring in both scoring and staging information. This is accomplished through a weighted constraint-based method that prioritizes solutions based on user-specified preferences, providing actionable insights for process improvement initiatives. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework through experimental results on real-world data, showing its potential to enhance predictive modeling efforts across various applications.
